name: SOC 2
also_known_as: SOC 2 Type I; SOC 2 Type II; Trust Services Criteria; TSC
source_note: AICPA SOC 2 examination under the Trust Services Criteria; Type I and Type II are report variants of one program
who_must_comply: B2B SaaS and technology service providers holding or processing customer data on behalf of business customers.
scope_summary: Covers the service organization's system boundary and the Trust Services Criteria selected (security is required; availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy are optional).
key_obligations_summary: Management defines the system, asserts control design and operation, and engages a licensed CPA firm to examine controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. Type 1 reports on design at a point in time; Type 2 reports on operating effectiveness over a period, commonly 3 to 12 months. The output is an attestation report rather than a pass/fail certificate.
typical_evidence_artifacts: policies|risk assessment|system description|control matrix|access reviews|change tickets|vendor reviews|penetration test|SOC 2 report
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; a qualified opinion, lapsed report or exceptions can breach customer contracts and stall or lose deals.
subordinate_controls_notes: Trust Services Criteria organized around control environment, communication, risk assessment, monitoring and control activities (COSO-aligned) plus logical access, operations, change management and risk mitigation criteria.

name: SOC 1
source_note: AICPA attestation on controls relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting
who_must_comply: Service providers whose systems affect customers' financial reporting, such as payroll, payments and billing platforms.
scope_summary: Covers controls relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) for the described service.
key_obligations_summary: Management describes the system and control objectives relevant to financial reporting and a CPA firm examines them under SSAE 18 (AT-C 320). Reports are issued as Type 1 (design) or Type 2 (design and operating effectiveness). User auditors rely on the report during their customers' financial audits.
typical_evidence_artifacts: system description|control objectives matrix|reconciliations|access reviews|change tickets|SOC 1 report
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; a missing or qualified report can force customers' auditors to expand testing and can breach service contracts.
subordinate_controls_notes: Control objectives are defined by the service organization around transaction processing, completeness, accuracy and IT general controls.

name: SOC 3
also_known_as: SOC 3 General Use Report; Trust Services Report for General Use
source_note: Public-facing general-use summary report derived from a SOC 2 examination
who_must_comply: Organizations that already hold a SOC 2 and want a public-facing trust summary.
scope_summary: Same scope as the underlying SOC 2 examination, presented as a general-use summary report.
key_obligations_summary: A SOC 3 report is a general-use version of a SOC 2 Type 2 engagement without the detailed test procedures and results. It can be published or posted publicly, unlike restricted-use SOC 2 reports. It does not replace a SOC 2 report in security reviews.
typical_evidence_artifacts: SOC 3 report|SOC 2 Type 2 report|system description
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; limited assurance value if buyers require the full SOC 2 report.
subordinate_controls_notes: Derived from the same Trust Services Criteria as the underlying SOC 2 engagement.

name: ISO/IEC 27001
source_note: Certifiable information security management system standard; current edition ISO/IEC 27001:2022
who_must_comply: Companies selling internationally or into ISO-preferring industries and geographies, and any organization wanting a certifiable security management system.
scope_summary: Applies to the information security management system (ISMS) scope the organization defines, including people, processes and technology inside that boundary.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a documented ISMS with leadership commitment, risk assessment and treatment, a Statement of Applicability covering Annex A controls, internal audit and management review. Certification is issued by an accredited certification body after Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits. Surveillance audits occur annually with full recertification every three years.
typical_evidence_artifacts: ISMS scope statement|risk assessment|risk treatment plan|Statement of Applicability|policies|internal audit reports|management review minutes|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; suspension or loss of the certificate can disqualify suppliers in RFPs and supplier portals.
subordinate_controls_notes: Clauses 4 to 10 define the management system; Annex A of the 2022 revision contains 93 controls in four themes (organizational, people, physical, technological).

name: ISO/IEC 27002
source_note: Guidance control set supporting ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A
who_must_comply: Organizations implementing or auditing information security controls, typically alongside an ISO 27001 ISMS.
scope_summary: Guidance standard covering the information security controls referenced by ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A.
key_obligations_summary: Provides implementation guidance and purpose statements for each control rather than certifiable management-system requirements. Organizations are not certified against ISO/IEC 27002 itself. It is commonly used to justify Statement of Applicability decisions.
typical_evidence_artifacts: control implementation guidance|Statement of Applicability|policies|control design documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: not applicable
penalties_summary: unknown
subordinate_controls_notes: The 2022 revision organizes 93 controls into organizational, people, physical and technological themes with attributes for filtering.

name: ISO/IEC 27017
source_note: Code of practice for information security controls for cloud services; linked catalogue entry is the 2015 edition, revised by ISO/IEC 27017:2026
who_must_comply: Cloud service providers and cloud customers that need cloud-specific security guidance on top of an ISMS.
scope_summary: Covers cloud service provider and cloud service customer responsibilities for information security in cloud environments.
key_obligations_summary: Provides cloud-specific implementation guidance for ISO/IEC 27002 controls plus additional cloud controls, including shared responsibility, virtual environment segregation and administrative operations. It is usually assessed as an extension to an ISO/IEC 27001 certification scope.
typical_evidence_artifacts: shared responsibility matrix|cloud control mapping|ISMS documentation|certificate annex
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: aligned to the ISO 27001 certification cycle
penalties_summary: unknown
subordinate_controls_notes: Adds cloud-specific guidance and supplementary controls layered on ISO/IEC 27002 control families.

name: ISO/IEC 27018
source_note: Code of practice for protecting personally identifiable information in public clouds acting as PII processors; linked entry is the 2019 edition, revised by ISO/IEC 27018:2025
who_must_comply: Public cloud providers acting as processors of personally identifiable information.
scope_summary: Covers PII protection controls for public cloud service providers processing personal data on behalf of customers.
key_obligations_summary: Provides a code of practice with additional controls and guidance for cloud processors, including transparency about subprocessors, data location and return or deletion of data. It is typically certified as an extension to an ISO/IEC 27001 scope. It does not by itself establish legal compliance with privacy laws.
typical_evidence_artifacts: subprocessor list|data location documentation|deletion and return procedures|ISMS documentation|certificate annex
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: aligned to the ISO 27001 certification cycle
penalties_summary: unknown
subordinate_controls_notes: Extends ISO/IEC 27002 with PII-specific controls for public cloud processors.

name: ISO/IEC 27701
also_known_as: ISO 27701; PIMS; privacy extension to ISO 27001
source_note: Privacy information management system requirements and guidance; current edition ISO/IEC 27701:2025
who_must_comply: Vendors processing significant volumes of personal data for global or privacy-sensitive customers, usually as an extension to ISO 27001.
scope_summary: Covers a Privacy Information Management System (PIMS) for organizations acting as PII controllers, PII processors or both, within a defined ISMS scope.
key_obligations_summary: Extends ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 with privacy-specific requirements and controls for controllers and processors, including purpose limitation, data subject rights handling, records of processing and transfer transparency. Certification requires an existing or concurrent ISO/IEC 27001 certification. Annexes map controls to GDPR articles, which supports but does not prove legal compliance.
typical_evidence_artifacts: PIMS documentation|records of processing|DPIA records|data subject rights procedures|DPA templates|internal audit reports|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; loss of the certificate can affect privacy-sensitive procurement and processor due diligence.
subordinate_controls_notes: Adds controller-specific and processor-specific control annexes on top of the ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 control set.

name: ISO/IEC 42001
source_note: Certifiable artificial intelligence management system standard
who_must_comply: Organizations developing, providing or using AI systems that need a certifiable AI governance management system.
scope_summary: Covers an AI management system (AIMS) for the AI systems and roles inside the declared scope, for providers and users of AI.
key_obligations_summary: Requires an AI management system with AI risk assessment, AI system impact assessment, defined roles across the AI lifecycle, and controls for data, model and third-party management. It is certifiable by accredited certification bodies. It is a governance standard and does not itself demonstrate conformity with AI legislation.
typical_evidence_artifacts: AIMS documentation|AI risk assessment|AI system impact assessment|model inventory|data governance records|internal audit reports|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; increasingly requested in AI procurement and RFPs.
subordinate_controls_notes: Clause structure mirrors other ISO management systems, with Annex A AI controls and Annex B implementation guidance.

name: ISO 22301
source_note: Business continuity management system requirements
who_must_comply: Organizations with availability or resilience commitments, including SaaS vendors facing continuity questions in security reviews.
scope_summary: Covers a business continuity management system (BCMS) for the products, services and sites in the declared scope.
key_obligations_summary: Requires business impact analysis, risk assessment, continuity strategies, documented plans, and exercising and testing of those plans. Certification is available from accredited bodies. Many buyers accept BCMS evidence without full certification.
typical_evidence_artifacts: business impact analysis|continuity plans|test and exercise reports|recovery objectives|management review minutes|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; unmet availability commitments can trigger SLA credits or contractual remedies.
subordinate_controls_notes: Management-system clauses with continuity-specific requirements for BIA, strategy, plans, exercising and evaluation.

name: ISO 9001
source_note: Quality management system requirements
who_must_comply: Manufacturers, service providers and suppliers in quality-gated supply chains, including some enterprise and public-sector tenders.
scope_summary: Covers a quality management system (QMS) for the products and services in the declared scope.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a process-based QMS with customer focus, documented processes, competence management, nonconformity and corrective action handling, internal audit and management review. Certification is issued by accredited certification bodies. It addresses quality management, not information security.
typical_evidence_artifacts: quality manual|process documentation|corrective action records|internal audit reports|management review minutes|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; loss of certification can remove a supplier from approved vendor lists.
subordinate_controls_notes: Clauses 4 to 10 cover context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement.

name: ISO 14001
source_note: Environmental management system requirements; current edition ISO 14001:2026
who_must_comply: Organizations with environmental commitments or customers, suppliers and tenders that require certified environmental management.
scope_summary: Covers an environmental management system (EMS) for the activities, products and services in the declared scope.
key_obligations_summary: Requires identification of environmental aspects and compliance obligations, environmental objectives, operational controls, emergency preparedness, internal audit and management review. Certification is issued by accredited certification bodies. It manages environmental performance rather than information security or privacy.
typical_evidence_artifacts: environmental policy|aspects and impacts register|legal register|objectives and targets|internal audit reports|management review minutes|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; loss of certification can affect supplier qualification and tender eligibility.
subordinate_controls_notes: Management-system clauses 4 to 10 with environmental aspects, compliance obligations and lifecycle perspective requirements.

name: ISO 13485
source_note: Quality management system requirements for medical device organizations
who_must_comply: Medical device manufacturers, and suppliers or software developers in the medical device supply chain, including software as a medical device.
scope_summary: Covers a quality management system for organizations involved in one or more stages of the medical device lifecycle.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a documented quality management system with design and development controls, risk management across the lifecycle, supplier controls, traceability, complaint handling and regulatory reporting processes. Certification supports regulatory approvals such as EU MDR conformity assessment and is widely expected by notified bodies. It is quality-system focused and does not replace product conformity assessment.
typical_evidence_artifacts: quality manual|design history file|risk management file|supplier evaluations|CAPA records|complaint and vigilance records|internal audit reports|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty directly; certification loss can block regulatory approvals and market access.
subordinate_controls_notes: Management-system clauses aligned with regulatory requirements, including design controls, risk management and post-market processes.

name: ISO/IEC 20000-1
also_known_as: ISO 20000; IT service management system; SMS
source_note: unverified-review-needed
who_must_comply: IT service providers and managed service organizations facing service management requirements in contracts.
scope_summary: Covers a service management system (SMS) for the services in the declared scope.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a documented service management system with service planning, service level management, incident, problem and change management, and continual improvement. Certification is available from accredited bodies. It complements but does not replace security certifications.
typical_evidence_artifacts: service catalog|SLAs|incident and change records|service reports|internal audit reports|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: unknown
subordinate_controls_notes: Management-system clauses plus service management process requirements such as SLM, incident, problem, change and release.

name: ISO 31000
source_note: Risk management principles and guidelines; guidance rather than certifiable requirements
who_must_comply: Organizations building an enterprise risk management approach, often to support other certifications.
scope_summary: Guidance for managing risk across any organization type, size or sector; not scoped to a specific system.
key_obligations_summary: Provides principles, a framework and a process for risk management including identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment, monitoring and communication. It is guidance only and is not certifiable. It is commonly referenced to justify risk methodology in ISO 27001 or SOC 2 programs.
typical_evidence_artifacts: risk management policy|risk methodology|risk register|risk treatment plan
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: not applicable
penalties_summary: unknown
subordinate_controls_notes: Not a control catalog; defines principles, framework and process elements for risk management.

name: ISA/IEC 62443
also_known_as: IEC 62443; industrial automation and control systems security
source_note: Series of standards for security of industrial automation and control systems
who_must_comply: Asset owners, system integrators and product suppliers involved in industrial automation and control systems, including OT-connected software vendors.
scope_summary: Covers industrial automation and control systems organized into zones and conduits, with roles for asset owners, integrators and product suppliers.
key_obligations_summary: Defines security program requirements for asset owners, security requirements for integration service providers, secure product development lifecycle requirements for suppliers, and technical system and component security requirements. Security levels 1 to 4 express the strength of protection required for each zone. Certification schemes such as ISASecure and IECEE assess products, processes and systems.
typical_evidence_artifacts: zone and conduit diagrams|risk assessment|secure development lifecycle documentation|security level target definitions|patch management plan|certification reports
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: certification cycles vary by scheme, commonly every 3 years
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty in most jurisdictions; frequently required contractually and referenced by sector regulators.
subordinate_controls_notes: Series structure covers general concepts, policies and procedures, system requirements including SR levels, and component requirements, with security levels SL 1 to SL 4.

name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
source_note: Voluntary risk-based cybersecurity framework, widely used internationally; CSF 2.0 published 2024
who_must_comply: Any organization wanting a common language for cybersecurity risk, frequently used as a baseline by SMBs and as a crosswalk by larger firms.
scope_summary: Voluntary framework applicable to organizations of any size or sector; scope is defined by the organization.
key_obligations_summary: Organizes cybersecurity outcomes into functions and categories that organizations use to assess current and target profiles. Version 2.0, published in 2024, added the Govern function alongside Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. It is outcome-based, so implementation is chosen by the organization and there is no certification.
typical_evidence_artifacts: current and target profile|gap assessment|risk register|policies|roadmap|control mapping
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual review recommended
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty on its own; adopted by reference in some contracts and sector rules.
subordinate_controls_notes: CSF 2.0 uses six functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), categories, subcategories, plus tiers and profiles; informative references map to other control sets.

name: NIST SP 800-53
also_known_as: SP 800-53 Rev. 5; security and privacy controls
source_note: Security and privacy control catalog for federal information systems; basis for FedRAMP baselines
who_must_comply: U.S. federal agencies and their systems, plus cloud providers pursuing FedRAMP and contractors that inherit the baselines.
scope_summary: Applies to federal information systems and organizations, and to non-federal systems where adopted by contract or program such as FedRAMP.
key_obligations_summary: Provides a catalog of security and privacy controls with low, moderate and high baselines selected by system categorization. Control selection is paired with assessment procedures in SP 800-53A. FedRAMP and FISMA programs use tailored baselines drawn from this catalog.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan|control implementation statements|assessment reports|POA&M|continuous monitoring reports
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous monitoring with periodic reassessment
penalties_summary: No direct fine; noncompliance can cause loss of authorization to operate, contract remedies or removal from federal programs.
subordinate_controls_notes: Twenty control families such as AC, AU, CM, IA, IR, RA, SC and SI, with baselines by impact level and overlays.

name: NIST SP 800-171
source_note: Requirements for protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in nonfederal systems
who_must_comply: Non-federal organizations, including defense and civilian contractors and their suppliers, that store, process or transmit Controlled Unclassified Information.
scope_summary: Applies to CUI in nonfederal systems and organizations, scoped to the environment where CUI is handled.
key_obligations_summary: Requires implementation of security requirements for protecting CUI, a system security plan and plans of action for gaps. DFARS 252.204-7012 obliges many defense contractors to implement it and report scores, and CMMC assessments verify it. Revision 3 restructured the requirement families and tailoring approach.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan|POA&M|self-assessment score|policies|CUI data flow diagram|assessment report
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: self-assessment at least annually; CMMC assessments every 3 years where required
penalties_summary: Contractual remedies including False Claims Act exposure for inaccurate representations, contract termination and loss of award eligibility.
subordinate_controls_notes: Security requirements grouped into families such as access control, audit and accountability, configuration management, identification and authentication, and incident response.

name: NIST SP 800-172
source_note: Enhanced security requirements supplementing SP 800-171 for high-value CUI
who_must_comply: Defense contractors handling CUI associated with critical programs or high value assets, where enhanced protection is specified.
scope_summary: Applies as a supplement to SP 800-171 for selected systems and components identified by the contracting agency.
key_obligations_summary: Provides enhanced security requirements aimed at advanced persistent threats, including penetration-resistant architecture and cyber resiliency measures. Requirements apply only when specified by the federal agency or contract. It is used for CMMC Level 3 assessment content.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan addendum|threat assessment|enhanced control evidence|assessment report
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: as specified by contract; CMMC Level 3 assessments every 3 years
penalties_summary: Contractual remedies including loss of award eligibility and contract termination.
subordinate_controls_notes: Enhanced requirements layered onto SP 800-171 families, focused on APT resilience, damage limitation and design-for-security.

name: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework
source_note: Secure software development practices referenced by US federal software attestation requirements
who_must_comply: Software producers, including SaaS vendors and suppliers to U.S. federal agencies subject to secure software attestation.
scope_summary: Covers secure software development practices across the software development lifecycle for the producer's software.
key_obligations_summary: Describes practices grouped into preparing the organization, protecting software, producing well-secured software and responding to vulnerabilities. It is referenced by U.S. federal secure software development attestation requirements for software sold to agencies. It is guidance rather than a certification.
typical_evidence_artifacts: secure SDLC policy|code review records|SAST and DAST results|SBOM|vulnerability disclosure policy|attestation form
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous with attestation when required by federal buyers
penalties_summary: For federal sales, inaccurate attestations can create False Claims Act and contract-remedy exposure; otherwise no statutory penalty.
subordinate_controls_notes: Practice groups PO (prepare organization), PS (protect software), PW (produce well-secured software) and RV (respond to vulnerabilities).

name: NIST Privacy Framework
source_note: Voluntary privacy risk management framework companion to the NIST CSF
who_must_comply: Organizations building a privacy risk management program, and, notably, controllers seeking the Tennessee affirmative defense tied to this framework.
scope_summary: Voluntary framework for managing privacy risk arising from data processing; scope is defined by the organization.
key_obligations_summary: Organizes privacy outcomes into functions and categories that organizations use to build current and target profiles alongside the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. It is voluntary, non-certifiable and technology-neutral. Tennessee's privacy statute provides an affirmative defense for programs that reasonably conform to it.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy risk assessment|current and target profile|data inventory|policies|privacy program documentation|gap remediation plan
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual review recommended
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; can support an affirmative defense under Tennessee's privacy law.
subordinate_controls_notes: Core functions Identify-P, Govern-P, Control-P, Communicate-P and Protect-P, with categories, subcategories, profiles and implementation tiers.

name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
source_note: Voluntary framework for managing risks of artificial intelligence systems
who_must_comply: Organizations designing, developing, deploying or using AI systems that need a voluntary AI risk management approach.
scope_summary: Voluntary framework for AI risks across the AI lifecycle; scope is set by the organization and AI use cases.
key_obligations_summary: Organizes AI risk management into the Govern, Map, Measure and Manage functions with characteristics of trustworthy AI. It is voluntary and not certifiable, and is often paired with the companion Playbook and generative AI profile. Many buyers use it as the structure for AI governance evidence.
typical_evidence_artifacts: AI use case inventory|AI risk assessment|model documentation|evaluation results|governance policy|incident process
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous with periodic review
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; used as a reference in contracts and emerging regulatory expectations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) with categories and subcategories, plus trustworthiness characteristics.

name: CIS Critical Security Controls
also_known_as: CIS Controls; CIS Top 18; Implementation Groups IG1-IG3
source_note: Prioritized cyber hygiene control set maintained by the Center for Internet Security
who_must_comply: Any company with systems, SaaS or customer data that needs a prioritized security baseline, especially SMBs and startups.
scope_summary: Applies to the enterprise's assets, accounts, data and networks; implementation groups scale scope by organization size and risk.
key_obligations_summary: Defines prioritized safeguards across 18 controls, grouped into Implementation Groups IG1 to IG3. IG1 is described as essential cyber hygiene for smaller organizations. The controls are voluntary, mapped to other frameworks, and not certifiable, though CIS offers self-assessment tooling.
typical_evidence_artifacts: asset inventory|configuration baselines|patch records|access reviews|backup tests|logging configuration|gap assessment
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual review recommended
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; gaps commonly become findings in questionnaires and audit readiness reviews.
subordinate_controls_notes: Eighteen controls with safeguards tiered across Implementation Groups IG1, IG2 and IG3.

name: CIS Benchmarks
source_note: Consensus secure configuration baselines for operating systems, cloud, and applications
who_must_comply: Any organization hardening operating systems, cloud services, containers, databases or network devices, often to satisfy audit configuration requirements.
scope_summary: Covers secure configuration baselines for specific technologies and versions rather than an organization-wide management system.
key_obligations_summary: Provides consensus-developed configuration recommendations with rationale, audit and remediation steps, generally organized into Level 1 and Level 2 profiles. Organizations select applicable benchmarks, document deviations and monitor drift, often using automated assessment tooling. There is no certification, though CIS Hardened Images and CIS-CAT support implementation and measurement.
typical_evidence_artifacts: hardening standards|configuration baselines|benchmark scan reports|deviation approvals|drift monitoring evidence
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; benchmarks updated by CIS and re-scanned periodically
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; unhardened configurations commonly become audit findings.
subordinate_controls_notes: Recommendations are grouped by technology with Level 1 and Level 2 profiles and optional STIG profiles for some platforms.

name: CSA STAR
also_known_as: Cloud Security Alliance STAR; CAIQ; Cloud Controls Matrix; CCM
source_note: Cloud assurance registry with self-assessment, certification, and attestation levels based on the Cloud Controls Matrix
who_must_comply: Cloud service providers and cloud-native SaaS vendors facing mature information security buyers.
scope_summary: Covers the cloud service offering assessed against the Cloud Controls Matrix, at the level of assurance chosen.
key_obligations_summary: Providers document controls against the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix and CAIQ and may publish results in the STAR Registry. Level 1 is self-assessment, Level 2 is third-party certification or attestation combined with ISO 27001 or SOC 2, and continuous monitoring options exist. Listing serves as a reusable trust artifact for cloud diligence.
typical_evidence_artifacts: CAIQ response|CCM control mapping|STAR registry listing|ISO 27001 certificate or SOC 2 report
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual for self-assessment; aligned to the underlying certification cycle for third-party levels
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; a stale registry entry undermines trust claims.
subordinate_controls_notes: Based on the Cloud Controls Matrix domains covering areas such as identity, encryption, logging, supply chain and application security, with assurance levels 1 and 2.

name: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard
source_note: Open application security requirements and verification standard used in secure development programs
who_must_comply: Development and security teams building or testing web applications and APIs.
scope_summary: Covers application-level security requirements for the application or API under review.
key_obligations_summary: Provides a catalog of verification requirements across levels of rigor that teams use for secure design, development and testing. It is a community standard with no formal certification body. It is often referenced in penetration test scopes and secure development policies.
typical_evidence_artifacts: secure design requirements|test plans|penetration test report|code review records|remediation tickets
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: per release or annual review
penalties_summary: unknown
subordinate_controls_notes: Requirements grouped by chapters such as authentication, session management, access control, validation and cryptography, tiered across verification levels.

name: PCI DSS
also_known_as: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard; PCI DSS v4.0.1
source_note: Card data security standard enforced contractually by payment brands and acquirers
who_must_comply: Merchants and service providers that store, process or transmit cardholder data, or that can affect the security of card transactions.
scope_summary: Covers the cardholder data environment, connected systems and any people and processes with access to account data.
key_obligations_summary: Requires implementation of technical and operational requirements across network security, data protection, vulnerability management, access control, monitoring and policy. Validation depends on merchant or service provider level and channel, using a Self-Assessment Questionnaire with an Attestation of Compliance or a Report on Compliance by a QSA. Version 4.0.1 is the current standard, with customized approach options and additional authentication and script-management requirements.
typical_evidence_artifacts: network diagrams|cardholder data flow diagram|scan reports (ASV)|penetration test report|policies|SAQ or ROC|Attestation of Compliance
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual validation with quarterly ASV scans
penalties_summary: Card brand fines and increased transaction fees passed through acquirers, plus liability for breach costs; amounts are set contractually.
subordinate_controls_notes: Twelve requirements grouped into six control objectives, with validation levels driven by transaction volume and channel and multiple SAQ types.

name: PCI Software Security Framework
also_known_as: PCI SSF; Secure Software Standard; Secure SLC Standard
source_note: Validation framework for payment software and secure software lifecycle; successor to PA-DSS
who_must_comply: Vendors that develop payment software sold, licensed or distributed to third parties, and organizations validating a secure software lifecycle.
scope_summary: Covers payment software products under the Secure Software Standard and vendor development processes under the Secure Software Lifecycle Standard.
key_obligations_summary: The Secure Software Standard sets security objectives for payment software including sensitive data protection, attack detection and secure updates, validated by a qualified assessor. The Secure SLC Standard validates the vendor's development lifecycle so qualifying changes can be released without full revalidation. Validated products and vendors are listed by the PCI Security Standards Council and the framework replaced PA-DSS.
typical_evidence_artifacts: secure SDLC documentation|threat models|test results|Report on Validation|listing on the PCI SSC website|change management records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: listing validity is typically 3 years with annual attestation
penalties_summary: No statutory fine; loss of listing affects the ability to sell validated payment software and can trigger customer contractual issues.
subordinate_controls_notes: Two standards: Secure Software Standard control objectives and Secure Software Lifecycle Standard process requirements, with optional modules such as terminal software.

name: PCI 3DS Core Security Standard
source_note: Security requirements for entities performing 3-D Secure functions; standards available in the PCI SSC document library
who_must_comply: Entities performing 3-D Secure functions such as access control servers, directory servers and 3DS servers.
scope_summary: Covers the 3DS environment and the systems, processes and personnel performing 3DS functions.
key_obligations_summary: Requires baseline security controls plus 3DS-specific requirements covering key management, transaction data protection and segregation of the 3DS environment. Assessment is performed by a qualified 3DS assessor, resulting in a Report on Compliance and Attestation of Compliance. It is generally applied in addition to, not instead of, PCI DSS where cardholder data is present.
typical_evidence_artifacts: 3DS environment diagrams|key management documentation|Report on Compliance|Attestation of Compliance|penetration test report|policies
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory fine; card brand and acquirer contractual consequences apply, including loss of ability to perform 3DS functions.
subordinate_controls_notes: Baseline security requirements plus 3DS security requirements, assessed against the 3DS Core Security Standard.

name: SWIFT Customer Security Programme
also_known_as: SWIFT CSP; Customer Security Controls Framework; CSCF
source_note: Mandatory control framework plus annual attestation for institutions on the Swift network
who_must_comply: Financial institutions and other entities connected to the Swift network, including service bureaus and their supporting technology providers.
scope_summary: Covers the user's Swift-related infrastructure and the architecture type declared, from full local footprint to fully outsourced connectivity.
key_obligations_summary: Requires implementation of the Customer Security Controls Framework, comprising mandatory and advisory controls scoped by architecture type. Users must submit an annual attestation through the KYC-Security Attestation application, supported by an independent assessment, either internal or external. Non-compliance can be reported to supervisors and to counterparties.
typical_evidence_artifacts: architecture type determination|control implementation evidence|independent assessment report|KYC-SA attestation|segregation and access records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No civil fine from Swift; non-compliance is reportable to supervisors and counterparties and can affect network access and correspondent relationships.
subordinate_controls_notes: Controls are organized into objectives and principles, split into mandatory and advisory controls scoped by architecture types A1 to B and the shared connectivity model.

name: HITRUST CSF
also_known_as: HITRUST Common Security Framework; e1; i1; r2
source_note: Certifiable control framework harmonizing HIPAA, NIST, ISO and other authoritative sources; heavily used in US healthcare
who_must_comply: Vendors selling to large healthcare systems, payers and other enterprises that mandate HITRUST certification.
scope_summary: Covers the in-scope systems and facilities assessed against the HITRUST CSF at the selected assessment type.
key_obligations_summary: Organizations scope requirements through the HITRUST MyCSF platform, implement the mapped control requirements and undergo validation by an authorized external assessor before HITRUST issues certification. Assessment types include the e1 essentials, i1 implemented and r2 risk-based options with differing rigor and validity. The CSF maps to multiple authoritative sources including HIPAA, NIST and ISO.
typical_evidence_artifacts: MyCSF scoping|policy and procedure documentation|control implementation evidence|validated assessment report|certification letter|corrective action plans
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: e1 and i1 annual; r2 every 2 years with interim assessment
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; loss of certification typically blocks HITRUST-gated healthcare procurement.
subordinate_controls_notes: CSF control categories with maturity scoring across policy, procedure and implemented levels; assessment tiers e1, i1 and r2.

name: FedRAMP
also_known_as: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program
source_note: US federal cloud security authorization program; baselines derived from NIST SP 800-53
who_must_comply: Cloud service providers selling cloud offerings to U.S. federal agencies.
scope_summary: Covers the cloud service offering boundary and its supporting infrastructure at the authorized impact level.
key_obligations_summary: Requires implementation of NIST SP 800-53 baselines tailored by FedRAMP, assessment by an accredited third-party assessment organization, and authorization by an agency or the FedRAMP program. Authorized offerings must maintain continuous monitoring with monthly deliverables and annual assessments. Impact levels are Low, Moderate and High, with FedRAMP Tailored options for lower-risk services.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan|Security Assessment Plan and Report|POA&M|penetration test report|monthly continuous monitoring deliverables|authorization letter
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual assessment with continuous monitoring
penalties_summary: No civil fine; without authorization agencies generally cannot procure the service, and authorization can be revoked.
subordinate_controls_notes: Baselines derived from NIST SP 800-53 control families at Low, Moderate and High impact levels, plus FedRAMP-specific parameters.

name: GovRAMP
also_known_as: StateRAMP; State Risk and Authorization Management Program
source_note: Cloud security verification program for US state, local, tribal, and education buyers; rebranded from StateRAMP to GovRAMP in February 2025
who_must_comply: Cloud vendors with U.S. state, local and education (SLED) sales motions where the program is required.
scope_summary: Covers the cloud offering boundary assessed at the required impact level for participating state and local governments.
key_obligations_summary: Uses NIST SP 800-53 based security requirements verified by a third-party assessment organization, with progressive statuses leading to Authorized. Verified offerings are listed for participating governments and require continuous monitoring. Requirements closely mirror FedRAMP, and FedRAMP packages can often be reciprocally recognized.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan|assessment report|POA&M|continuous monitoring deliverables|StateRAMP status listing
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual assessment with continuous monitoring
penalties_summary: No civil fine; missing status can disqualify bids in procurements that require it.
subordinate_controls_notes: Security requirements based on NIST SP 800-53 baselines at Low, Moderate and High categorizations, with Ready, Provisional and Authorized statuses.

name: TX-RAMP
also_known_as: Texas Risk and Authorization Management Program
source_note: Statutory Texas cloud certification program required for state agency cloud contracts under Tex. Gov't Code 2054.0593
who_must_comply: Cloud service providers contracting with Texas state agencies or institutions of higher education.
scope_summary: Covers cloud computing services that process, store or transmit Texas state agency data, categorized by impact level.
key_obligations_summary: Requires certification at Level 1 for higher-impact data or Level 2 for lower-impact data, based on evidence such as a StateRAMP or FedRAMP authorization, or a Texas-specific assessment package. State agencies may not enter or renew contracts for cloud services that lack the required status. The Department of Information Resources manages the program and publishes certified services.
typical_evidence_artifacts: TX-RAMP application|System Security Plan|assessment evidence or reciprocal FedRAMP/StateRAMP package|POA&M|continuous monitoring deliverables|certification listing
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: certification is typically valid for 3 years with continuous monitoring
penalties_summary: No civil fine; state agencies are prohibited from contracting for non-certified cloud services, which blocks Texas public-sector revenue.
subordinate_controls_notes: Two certification levels based on data impact, with controls derived from NIST SP 800-53 through the StateRAMP model.

name: Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification
source_note: DoD program for contractors handling Federal Contract Information and Controlled Unclassified Information; Phase II third-party assessment requirements suspended July 2026 pending reform review, Phase I self-assessments remain
who_must_comply: Defense contractors and subcontractors in the Defense Industrial Base that handle Federal Contract Information or Controlled Unclassified Information.
scope_summary: Applies to the contractor systems that process, store or transmit FCI or CUI, scoped to the assessment boundary.
key_obligations_summary: Establishes three levels: Level 1 self-assessment for FCI based on FAR 52.204-21, Level 2 based on NIST SP 800-171 (self or C3PAO certification assessment), and Level 3 adding selected NIST SP 800-172 requirements assessed by DCMA DIBCAC. Contractors must post results and affirmations in SPRS. Required levels are set in solicitations under the DoD acquisition rule.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan|POA&M|SPRS score and affirmation|CUI asset inventory|assessment report|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual affirmations
penalties_summary: Loss of contract eligibility, contract termination, and False Claims Act exposure for false representations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Three levels; Level 1 covers 15 FAR basic safeguarding requirements, Level 2 covers the NIST SP 800-171 requirement families, Level 3 adds selected SP 800-172 enhanced requirements.

name: Federal Information Security Modernization Act
issuing_body: US Congress; overseen by CISA and OMB
source_note: Statutory information security requirements for US federal agencies and their contractors
who_must_comply: U.S. federal agencies and contractors operating information systems on behalf of an agency.
scope_summary: Applies to federal information and information systems, including contractor systems used or operated for an agency.
key_obligations_summary: Requires agencies to run an information security program with system categorization under FIPS 199, control selection from NIST SP 800-53, assessment and authorization, and continuous monitoring. Agencies report annually to OMB and Congress. Contractors inherit requirements through contract terms.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan|risk assessment|assessment report|POA&M|authorization to operate|continuous monitoring reports
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous monitoring with annual reporting and periodic reauthorization
penalties_summary: No civil fine on contractors directly; consequences include loss of authorization to operate, budget and oversight actions, and contract remedies.
subordinate_controls_notes: Implemented through the NIST Risk Management Framework and SP 800-53 control families.

name: DFARS 252.204-7012
source_note: Defense contract clause requiring NIST SP 800-171 implementation and 72-hour cyber incident reporting
who_must_comply: U.S. Department of Defense contractors and subcontractors whose contracts involve covered defense information.
scope_summary: Applies to covered contractor information systems that process, store or transmit covered defense information.
key_obligations_summary: Requires implementation of NIST SP 800-171 security requirements, rapid reporting of cyber incidents to DoD within 72 hours, media preservation, malicious software submission and flow-down to subcontractors. Cloud services used to store covered defense information must generally meet DoD cloud security requirements. It is imposed through the contract clause.
typical_evidence_artifacts: System Security Plan|POA&M|incident reports to DIBNet|subcontract flow-down clauses|SPRS score
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; assessments per contract and CMMC cycle
penalties_summary: Contract remedies including termination, withholding of payment, and False Claims Act exposure for misrepresentation.
subordinate_controls_notes: Points to the NIST SP 800-171 requirement families plus incident reporting and flow-down obligations.

name: International Traffic in Arms Regulations
source_note: Export controls on defense articles, services, and technical data; drives US-person access and data residency controls
who_must_comply: U.S. persons and companies that manufacture, export, broker or handle defense articles, defense services or technical data on the U.S. Munitions List.
scope_summary: Applies to defense articles and technical data on the USML, including software and technical data shared with foreign persons, wherever located.
key_obligations_summary: Requires registration with the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls for manufacturers, exporters and brokers, licensing or use of exemptions for exports and re-exports, and controls preventing deemed exports to foreign persons. Recordkeeping and access controls over technical data are required, including for cloud environments. Compliance programs commonly include personnel screening and encryption practices.
typical_evidence_artifacts: DDTC registration|export licenses and agreements|technical data access controls|screening records|export recordkeeping|compliance manual
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual registration renewal; continuous compliance
penalties_summary: Civil penalties per violation and criminal penalties up to one million U.S. dollars and up to twenty years imprisonment per willful violation, plus debarment.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured by USML categories and ITAR parts covering registration, licensing, exemptions, brokering and recordkeeping.

name: Export Administration Regulations
also_known_as: EAR; 15 CFR Parts 730-774; dual-use export controls
issuing_body: US Bureau of Industry and Security
source_note: Dual-use export controls affecting encryption, cloud access, and technology transfer; official eCFR text administered by BIS
who_must_comply: U.S. and, through extraterritorial rules, some non-U.S. companies exporting or transferring commercial and dual-use items, software and technology.
scope_summary: Applies to items subject to the EAR, including those on the Commerce Control List and EAR99 items, and to deemed exports of technology to foreign nationals.
key_obligations_summary: Requires classification of items, determination of license requirements by country, end user and end use, screening against restricted party lists, and recordkeeping. Encryption software has specific classification and reporting rules. License exceptions may apply but must be documented.
typical_evidence_artifacts: item classification (ECCN) records|license determinations|restricted party screening logs|export records|encryption self-classification reports|compliance manual
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; periodic program review recommended
penalties_summary: Administrative monetary penalties per violation, denial of export privileges, and criminal penalties for willful violations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Organized by Commerce Control List categories and product groups with country charts and license exceptions.

name: Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act
source_note: Accessibility requirements for US federal ICT procurement; incorporates WCAG success criteria
who_must_comply: U.S. federal agencies and, in practice, vendors selling information and communication technology to them.
scope_summary: Covers ICT developed, procured, maintained or used by federal agencies, including software, websites, documents and hardware.
key_obligations_summary: Requires ICT to conform to the Revised 508 Standards, which incorporate WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA success criteria for web and non-web content plus hardware and support documentation requirements. Vendors typically document conformance in an Accessibility Conformance Report based on the VPAT template. Agencies must assess and report on accessibility, and procurement can be challenged for non-conforming ICT.
typical_evidence_artifacts: Accessibility Conformance Report (VPAT)|automated and manual test results|remediation roadmap|accessibility policy|training records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: reassessed per release and at procurement; agency reporting is periodic
penalties_summary: No direct fine; consequences include lost or challenged federal awards and administrative complaints or civil actions under the Rehabilitation Act.
subordinate_controls_notes: Revised 508 Standards adopt WCAG 2.0 A and AA success criteria along with functional performance criteria and hardware, software and support documentation chapters.

name: Americans with Disabilities Act
also_known_as: ADA; ADA Title II web accessibility rule
source_note: Civil rights statute driving digital accessibility obligations and litigation risk for public accommodations
who_must_comply: Places of public accommodation under Title III, employers under Title I, and state and local governments and their vendors under Title II.
scope_summary: Covers discrimination on the basis of disability, applied by courts and DOJ rulemaking to websites, mobile apps and other digital services.
key_obligations_summary: Requires that goods, services and programs be accessible to people with disabilities, including effective communication and reasonable modifications. The 2024 Title II rule requires state and local government web content and mobile apps to conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, with compliance dates in 2026 and 2027 depending on entity size. For private businesses under Title III there is no codified technical standard, so WCAG conformance is the prevailing benchmark used in litigation and settlements.
typical_evidence_artifacts: accessibility policy|Accessibility Conformance Report (VPAT)|audit and remediation records|user testing results|training records|barrier removal plan
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; audits commonly annual and per major release
penalties_summary: Private plaintiffs may obtain injunctive relief and attorney fees, and some state laws add damages; DOJ civil penalties for Title III violations are set by regulation and adjusted for inflation, exceeding 100,000 US dollars for subsequent violations.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; digital conformance is evaluated against WCAG success criteria, with the Title II rule specifying WCAG 2.1 Level AA.

name: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
source_note: Technical accessibility success criteria referenced by ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549, and the EU Accessibility Act
who_must_comply: Any organization producing web or digital content, especially those subject to ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549 or the European Accessibility Act.
scope_summary: Covers web content, including web applications, documents and, through WCAG2ICT guidance, non-web software and content.
key_obligations_summary: Organizes accessibility requirements under the perceivable, operable, understandable and robust principles, with testable success criteria at conformance levels A, AA and AAA. Level AA is the common regulatory and contractual benchmark. Conformance is self-declared or evaluated by specialists, since there is no certification body.
typical_evidence_artifacts: Accessibility Conformance Report (VPAT)|automated scan results|manual and assistive technology test results|remediation backlog|design system accessibility documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: per release; full audits commonly annual
penalties_summary: No penalty in itself; non-conformance drives liability under accessibility laws that reference it.
subordinate_controls_notes: Four principles, thirteen guidelines and success criteria graded at levels A, AA and AAA; WCAG 2.2 adds criteria to WCAG 2.1.

name: UK G-Cloud Framework
also_known_as: Digital Marketplace G-Cloud; Crown Commercial Service G-Cloud
source_note: UK public sector cloud procurement framework (agreement RM1557.14, G-Cloud 14) with supplier assurance and terms obligations
who_must_comply: Suppliers selling cloud hosting, software or support to UK public-sector buyers through the Crown Commercial Service framework.
scope_summary: Covers services listed on the framework and the associated framework and call-off contract terms, not a security control set.
key_obligations_summary: Suppliers apply during a framework iteration, submit service definitions, pricing and terms, and must keep listings accurate. Call-off contracts impose obligations that commonly include security, data protection, transparency and exit assistance, and buyers frequently require Cyber Essentials or equivalent assurance. Listings are only valid for the framework term, so re-application is needed for successor iterations.
typical_evidence_artifacts: service definition documents|pricing documents|framework agreement|call-off contract|security questionnaire responses|Cyber Essentials certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: per framework iteration, historically about every 12 to 18 months
penalties_summary: No statutory fine; removal from the framework or contract termination ends public-sector sales through that route.
subordinate_controls_notes: Not a control framework; obligations flow from framework and call-off terms plus buyer-specific assurance requirements.

name: Cyber Essentials
source_note: UK government-backed baseline cyber certification; Plus adds hands-on technical verification
who_must_comply: Vendors selling to UK government and to UK private buyers that require the scheme, including many public-sector tenders.
scope_summary: Covers internet-facing infrastructure, devices, software and user accounts within the declared organizational scope.
key_obligations_summary: Requires implementation of five technical control themes: firewalls, secure configuration, security update management, user access control and malware protection. Basic certification is a verified self-assessment; Cyber Essentials Plus adds hands-on technical verification by an assessor. Certification is valid for twelve months.
typical_evidence_artifacts: self-assessment questionnaire|asset and software inventory|patch evidence|MFA configuration|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory fine; expired or missing certification can disqualify suppliers from UK tenders that mandate it.
subordinate_controls_notes: Five control themes; two levels (Cyber Essentials and Cyber Essentials Plus) with the Plus level independently tested.

name: Infosec Registered Assessors Program
source_note: ASD-endorsed independent security assessment against the Australian Information Security Manual
who_must_comply: Vendors and cloud providers seeking to handle Australian government information.
scope_summary: Covers the system or service assessed against the Australian Government Information Security Manual controls at the relevant classification level.
key_obligations_summary: An IRAP-endorsed assessor evaluates the system against the ISM controls and produces a security assessment report; the government entity then makes its own risk-based authorization decision. IRAP is an assessment process, not a certification issued by the ASD. Scope and classification level determine applicable controls.
typical_evidence_artifacts: system security plan|ISM control matrix|IRAP assessment report|risk management plan|POA&M
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: typically every 24 months or on significant change
penalties_summary: No direct fine; agencies may decline to use unassessed services.
subordinate_controls_notes: Controls come from the Australian Government Information Security Manual, with Essential Eight maturity levels frequently assessed alongside.

name: ACSC Essential Eight
source_note: Prioritized mitigation strategies and maturity model used across Australian government and industry
who_must_comply: Australian organizations, including government suppliers, expected to demonstrate baseline cyber mitigation maturity.
scope_summary: Applies to the organization's internet-connected IT environment; maturity levels scale with threat sophistication.
key_obligations_summary: Defines eight mitigation strategies including application control, patching applications and operating systems, configuring macro settings, user application hardening, restricting administrative privileges, multi-factor authentication and regular backups. Maturity Levels One to Three describe increasing rigor. Non-corporate Commonwealth entities are directed to implement it, and it is widely used commercially as a baseline.
typical_evidence_artifacts: maturity assessment|patch records|application control configuration|MFA configuration|backup test records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual assessment commonly expected
penalties_summary: No direct fine for private entities; government entities face compliance reporting and directive obligations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Eight mitigation strategies assessed against Maturity Levels One, Two and Three.

name: BSI Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue
issuing_body: German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI)
source_note: German government cloud criteria catalogue audited via ISAE 3000 type attestation reports
who_must_comply: Cloud service providers selling into German and DACH markets, especially to public sector and regulated customers.
scope_summary: Covers the cloud service in scope against the BSI Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue.
key_obligations_summary: Providers are assessed by an auditor against the C5 criteria and receive an attestation report based on ISAE 3000 style engagements, issued as Type 1 or Type 2. The catalogue includes basic and additional criteria plus mandatory environmental disclosures about jurisdiction and data location. German federal customers frequently require C5 attestation.
typical_evidence_artifacts: C5 attestation report|system description|control matrix|environmental disclosures|penetration test report
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory fine for private providers; absence commonly blocks German public-sector and regulated procurement.
subordinate_controls_notes: Criteria organized into control domains with basic and additional criteria, plus supplementary environmental information requirements.

name: Esquema Nacional de Seguridad
also_known_as: ENS; Spanish National Security Framework; Real Decreto 311/2022
source_note: Mandatory Spanish security framework for public administrations and their private-sector suppliers
who_must_comply: Spanish public sector entities and private-sector suppliers providing services or systems to them.
scope_summary: Covers information systems used to provide services to Spanish public administrations, categorized as basic, medium or high.
key_obligations_summary: Requires system categorization, a risk analysis, a declaration or certification of conformity, and implementation of the security measures in Annex II appropriate to the category. Basic-category systems may use a self-declaration, while medium and high categories require certification by an accredited conformity assessment entity. Conformity must be published and maintained.
typical_evidence_artifacts: system categorization|risk analysis|security policy|Statement of Applicability|conformity declaration or certificate|continuous improvement records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: certification is typically valid for 2 years with periodic audit
penalties_summary: No general fine schedule for suppliers; without conformity, public-sector contracts and system operation are blocked, and public bodies face administrative consequences.
subordinate_controls_notes: Security measures in Annex II grouped into organizational, operational and protection measures, scaled by basic, medium and high categories.

name: ISMAP
also_known_as: Information system Security Management and Assessment Program
issuing_body: ISMAP Steering Committee (Digital Agency, METI, MIC)
source_note: Japanese government cloud service security assessment and registration program
who_must_comply: Cloud service providers seeking to sell cloud services to Japanese government agencies.
scope_summary: Covers the registered cloud service and its management, operational and technical controls, with a separate lighter track for low-risk services.
key_obligations_summary: Providers implement the ISMAP control criteria, undergo an audit by an ISMAP-registered auditing firm, and apply for registration on the ISMAP cloud service list maintained by the steering committee. Government procurement is generally limited to registered services. Registration must be renewed through periodic audits and updated for significant changes.
typical_evidence_artifacts: control implementation documentation|internal audit records|external audit report|application and registration records|risk assessment
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual audit and renewal
penalties_summary: No civil fine; without registration, Japanese government procurement is generally not available.
subordinate_controls_notes: Control criteria derived from ISO/IEC 27001, 27002, 27017 and NIST SP 800-53, split into governance, management and operational and technical controls, with an ISMAP-LIU track for low-impact services.

name: ISMS-P (Korea)
also_known_as: K-ISMS; K-ISMS-P; Personal Information and Information Security Management System
source_note: Korean statutory certification for information security and personal information management systems, operated by KISA
who_must_comply: Korean information and communications service providers meeting statutory thresholds, plus organizations voluntarily certifying, including foreign providers serving Korea.
scope_summary: Covers the certified management system scope, either ISMS for information security or ISMS-P which adds personal information protection.
key_obligations_summary: Requires implementation of management system requirements and control items, an internal review, and certification audit by an authorized certification body under KISA and the PIPC. Certain service providers are legally required to obtain ISMS certification based on revenue and user thresholds. Certificates are valid for three years with annual follow-up audits.
typical_evidence_artifacts: management system documentation|risk assessment|control implementation evidence|internal review records|certification audit report|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual follow-up audits
penalties_summary: Fines of up to 30 million Korean won for failing to obtain mandatory ISMS certification, alongside separate PIPA penalties for privacy violations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Management system requirements plus control items in ISMS and additional personal information lifecycle controls in the ISMS-P scope.

name: Multi-Tier Cloud Security Singapore Standard
issuing_body: Infocomm Media Development Authority; Singapore Standards Council
source_note: Three-tier cloud security certification required for Singapore government public cloud bulk tenders; official IMDA factsheet
who_must_comply: Cloud service providers serving Singapore government and regulated customers, particularly for bulk tender eligibility.
scope_summary: Covers the cloud service and supporting infrastructure certified at Level 1, 2 or 3 according to data sensitivity and business impact.
key_obligations_summary: Providers implement the SS 584 controls for the target tier and are certified by an accredited certification body. Level 3 is aimed at regulated and high-impact workloads and includes the most extensive control set. Certification is accompanied by a self-disclosure schedule that customers use for due diligence.
typical_evidence_artifacts: control implementation documentation|self-disclosure schedule|certification audit report|certificate|risk assessment
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits
penalties_summary: No statutory fine; missing certification can exclude providers from Singapore government cloud tenders.
subordinate_controls_notes: Controls organized by domain across three cumulative tiers, with Level 3 adding the strictest requirements.

name: TISAX
also_known_as: Trusted Information Security Assessment Exchange; VDA ISA
source_note: Automotive-sector information security assessment and result-exchange mechanism based on the VDA ISA catalogue
who_must_comply: Suppliers and service providers in the automotive industry supply chain, including software vendors serving OEMs.
scope_summary: Covers the sites and services in the declared assessment scope against the VDA ISA catalogue at the required assessment level.
key_obligations_summary: Participants perform a VDA ISA self-assessment, undergo an audit by an accredited provider at the required assessment level, and share results through the ENX exchange rather than receiving a public certificate. Assessment objectives cover information security, prototype protection and data protection depending on scope. Labels are typically valid for three years.
typical_evidence_artifacts: VDA ISA self-assessment|assessment report|TISAX labels|policies|prototype protection controls
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years
penalties_summary: No statutory fine; missing labels typically block automotive supplier onboarding and contracts.
subordinate_controls_notes: Based on the VDA Information Security Assessment catalogue with assessment levels AL 1 to AL 3 and modules for information security, prototype protection and data protection.

name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule
source_note: Parental consent and data handling requirements for online services directed to children under 13
who_must_comply: Operators of websites, apps and online services directed to children under 13, and operators with actual knowledge that they collect personal information from children under 13.
scope_summary: Applies to online collection, use and disclosure of personal information from children under 13, including through third-party services integrated into child-directed properties.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a clear online privacy notice, direct notice and verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children, and a means for parents to review or delete data and revoke consent. Operators must limit collection to what is reasonably necessary, retain data only as long as needed, and maintain reasonable security including vendor assurances. The amended COPPA Rule adds requirements such as a written children's data security program and separate consent for third-party disclosures including targeted advertising.
typical_evidence_artifacts: child-directed determination|privacy notice|parental consent records|data retention policy|vendor agreements|security program documentation|deletion request logs
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; retention and security program reviewed at least annually
penalties_summary: FTC civil penalties of up to the statutory maximum per violation, adjusted annually for inflation and currently over 50,000 US dollars per violation, plus injunctive relief.
subordinate_controls_notes: Rule sections cover notice, parental consent, parental rights, confidentiality and security, and safe harbor programs.

name: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act
source_note: Student education records privacy law flowing down to school-service vendors under the school official exception
who_must_comply: U.S. educational agencies and institutions receiving Department of Education funding, and vendors acting as school officials under their direct control.
scope_summary: Applies to education records containing personally identifiable information about students held by covered schools and their designated school officials.
key_obligations_summary: Requires parental or eligible-student consent before disclosing personally identifiable information from education records, unless an exception such as the school official exception applies. Vendors relying on that exception must use the data only for authorized purposes, remain under the school's direct control and not redisclose without authorization. Schools must provide annual notification of rights and allow inspection, review and amendment requests.
typical_evidence_artifacts: district data privacy agreement|annual notification of rights|data use limitations documentation|subprocessor list|deletion and return procedures|training records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; contracts and notices reviewed annually
penalties_summary: No monetary fine; the Department of Education may require corrective action and can ultimately withhold federal funding, and vendors may face a five-year prohibition on access after certain violations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are structured by disclosure exceptions and recordkeeping duties in 34 CFR Part 99 rather than technical control families.

name: CAN-SPAM Act
source_note: Commercial email requirements covering headers, unsubscribe, physical address, and deceptive content
who_must_comply: Any organization sending commercial email messages that promote a product or service to U.S. recipients, including B2B senders.
scope_summary: Applies to commercial electronic mail messages, with lighter rules for transactional or relationship messages, regardless of whether the list is opt-in.
key_obligations_summary: Requires accurate header and sender information, non-deceptive subject lines, identification of the message as an advertisement where applicable, a valid physical postal address, and a clear opt-out mechanism. Opt-out requests must be honored within ten business days and the mechanism must remain functional for at least 30 days after sending. Senders remain responsible for compliance by affiliates and agents acting on their behalf.
typical_evidence_artifacts: email templates with identification and address|unsubscribe workflow evidence|suppression list|sending policy|affiliate and vendor agreements
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous
penalties_summary: FTC civil penalties of up to the statutory maximum per non-compliant email, adjusted annually for inflation and currently over 50,000 US dollars per email, with aggravated violations subject to additional liability.
subordinate_controls_notes: Requirements are organized around header accuracy, identification, opt-out and physical address rather than control families.

name: Telephone Consumer Protection Act
also_known_as: TCPA; 47 CFR 64.1200; robocall and SMS consent rules
source_note: Consent requirements for calls, texts, and faxes; significant private-right-of-action exposure
who_must_comply: Any business placing calls or sending text messages or faxes to U.S. numbers, including SaaS platforms enabling such messaging on customers' behalf.
scope_summary: Applies to calls and texts using an automatic telephone dialing system or artificial or prerecorded voice, telemarketing to residential and wireless numbers, and unsolicited fax advertisements.
key_obligations_summary: Requires prior express consent for many automated calls and texts, and prior express written consent for marketing calls and texts to wireless numbers and for artificial or prerecorded telemarketing calls. Callers must honor do-not-call requests, screen against the National Do Not Call Registry for telemarketing, provide identification and an opt-out mechanism, and observe calling-time restrictions. FCC rules also require revocation of consent to be honored promptly, generally within ten business days.
typical_evidence_artifacts: consent capture records|do-not-call and revocation logs|calling scripts and disclosures|vendor agreements|complaint handling records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous
penalties_summary: Statutory damages of 500 US dollars per violation, trebled up to 1,500 US dollars for willful or knowing violations, with an active private right of action and class-action exposure, plus FCC forfeitures.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations derive from the statute and FCC rules in 47 CFR 64.1200 covering consent, identification and do-not-call requirements.

name: Fair Credit Reporting Act
source_note: Governs consumer reports, background screening, and furnisher obligations
who_must_comply: Consumer reporting agencies, users of consumer reports such as employers and lenders, and furnishers of information to consumer reporting agencies.
scope_summary: Applies to consumer reports used for credit, employment, insurance, tenancy and other permissible purposes, including background screening and some data analytics products.
key_obligations_summary: Requires permissible purpose for obtaining consumer reports, disclosure and written authorization for employment screening, and pre-adverse and adverse action notices with a copy of the report and summary of rights. Consumer reporting agencies must follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy, investigate disputes and honor consumer file access rights. Furnishers must provide accurate information and investigate disputed items.
typical_evidence_artifacts: permissible purpose certifications|disclosure and authorization forms|adverse action notice templates|dispute handling records|accuracy procedures|vendor agreements
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; policies reviewed periodically
penalties_summary: Statutory damages of 100 to 1,000 US dollars per willful violation plus punitive damages and attorney fees, actual damages for negligent violations, and FTC or CFPB civil penalties.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are organized by role: consumer reporting agency, user of reports and furnisher of information.

name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act
source_note: Biometric consent, retention, and disclosure statute with a private right of action
who_must_comply: Private entities that collect or possess biometric identifiers or biometric information from individuals in Illinois, including employers using biometric timekeeping.
scope_summary: Applies to biometric identifiers such as fingerprints, voiceprints, retina or iris scans and face geometry, and to biometric information derived from them.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a written, publicly available retention and destruction policy, informed written consent before collection, and a prohibition on selling or profiting from biometric data. Disclosure to third parties generally requires consent, and entities must store biometric data using the reasonable standard of care applicable to their industry. Illinois amended the statute in 2024 so that repeated collections of the same biometric from the same person generally give rise to a single violation.
typical_evidence_artifacts: written release and consent records|retention and destruction schedule|public biometric policy|vendor agreements|deletion evidence|security documentation
