renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; destruction when purpose is satisfied or within three years of last interaction
penalties_summary: Statutory damages of 1,000 US dollars per negligent violation and 5,000 US dollars per intentional or reckless violation, or actual damages if greater, with a private right of action and attorney fees.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations center on notice, written consent, retention policy, prohibition on sale and security standards.

name: Washington My Health My Data Act
issuing_body: Washington State Legislature; Washington Attorney General
source_note: Consumer health data law codified at RCW chapter 19.373, with consent and authorization requirements plus a private right of action
who_must_comply: Legal entities that conduct business in Washington or target Washington consumers and that collect, process, share or sell consumer health data, excluding HIPAA-covered data and government agencies.
scope_summary: Applies to consumer health data, defined broadly to include information that identifies a consumer's past, present or future physical or mental health status, including inferences and precise location near health facilities.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a separate consumer health data privacy policy, opt-in consent for collection and sharing beyond what is necessary for a requested product or service, and separate valid authorization to sell such data. Consumers have rights to confirm, access, withdraw consent and delete their health data, including deletion by downstream recipients. Geofencing around in-person health service locations for advertising or data collection is prohibited.
typical_evidence_artifacts: consumer health data privacy policy|consent and authorization records|deletion request workflow|data inventory|vendor and processor contracts|geofencing controls
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous
penalties_summary: Enforced as a Consumer Protection Act violation by the Attorney General, with a private right of action; CPA civil penalties reach up to 7,500 US dollars per violation.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are organized around notice, consent, authorization for sale, consumer rights and the geofencing prohibition.

name: NYC Local Law 144
also_known_as: NYC AEDT Law; automated employment decision tools bias audit
issuing_body: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
source_note: Requires annual independent bias audits and candidate notice for automated employment decision tools
who_must_comply: Employers and employment agencies using automated employment decision tools for hiring or promotion decisions concerning candidates and employees in New York City.
scope_summary: Covers automated employment decision tools used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decisions for NYC-based positions.
key_obligations_summary: Requires an independent bias audit within one year before use, calculating selection or scoring rates and impact ratios by sex and race or ethnicity categories, with a public summary of results posted on the employer's website. Candidates and employees must receive at least ten business days' notice before use, including the job qualifications and characteristics assessed. Enforcement is by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.
typical_evidence_artifacts: independent bias audit report|published audit summary|candidate notices|tool inventory|vendor documentation and data|record retention
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual bias audit
penalties_summary: Civil penalties of up to 500 US dollars for a first violation and 500 to 1,500 US dollars for each subsequent violation, with each day of continued non-compliant use treated as a separate violation.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations center on the bias audit methodology, publication and candidate notice.

name: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act
source_note: Notice, consent, and reporting duties when AI analyzes video interviews of applicants
who_must_comply: Employers that use artificial intelligence to analyze video interviews of applicants for positions based in Illinois.
scope_summary: Covers AI analysis of applicant video interviews, including the notice, consent, sharing and deletion of those recordings.
key_obligations_summary: Requires notifying applicants before the interview that AI may be used, explaining how the AI works and what characteristics it evaluates, and obtaining consent. Videos may be shared only with persons whose expertise is necessary to evaluate the applicant, and must be deleted, including backups, within 30 days of an applicant's deletion request. Employers that rely solely on AI to decide who advances to in-person interviews must collect and report race and ethnicity data annually to the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity.
typical_evidence_artifacts: applicant notice and explanation|consent records|deletion evidence|sharing logs|annual demographic report where applicable|vendor documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; demographic reporting annual where applicable
penalties_summary: The Act does not specify monetary penalties; enforcement exposure arises through related Illinois employment and civil rights laws, so the specific penalty amount is unknown.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations cover notice, explanation, consent, sharing limits, deletion and demographic reporting.

name: California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by CPRA
also_known_as: CCPA; CPRA; California Privacy Rights Act
issuing_body: California Privacy Protection Agency; California Attorney General
source_note: First US comprehensive state privacy law; CPRA added sensitive data, sharing opt-out, and a dedicated regulator
who_must_comply: For-profit businesses that do business in California and meet a threshold: over 25 million US dollars in annual gross revenue, buying, selling or sharing personal information of 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or deriving 50 percent or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information.
scope_summary: Applies to personal information of California residents, including employees, job applicants and business contacts, with entity- and data-level exemptions such as HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data.
key_obligations_summary: Requires notices at collection and a comprehensive privacy policy, and support for rights to know, delete, correct, opt out of sale or sharing, limit use of sensitive personal information and non-discrimination. Businesses must honor opt-out preference signals such as Global Privacy Control, provide a Do Not Sell or Share link where applicable, and use compliant contracts with service providers, contractors and third parties. Risk assessments, cybersecurity audits and automated decision-making rules apply under CPPA regulations on a phased timeline.
typical_evidence_artifacts: notice at collection|privacy policy|consumer rights request log|opt-out preference signal handling|service provider contracts|data inventory|risk assessments|cybersecurity audit records|training records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; privacy policy updated at least every 12 months, with annual cybersecurity audits phased in for in-scope businesses
penalties_summary: Administrative or civil penalties of 2,500 US dollars per violation and 7,500 US dollars per intentional violation or violation involving a minor's data, plus a private right of action for certain data breaches with statutory damages of 100 to 750 US dollars per consumer per incident.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations cover notices, consumer rights, opt-out signals, sensitive data limits, contracts and, under CPPA regulations, risk assessments, cybersecurity audits and automated decision-making technology.

name: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act

scope_summary: Applies to personal data of Virginia residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Nonprofits and institutions of higher education are exempt.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on January 1, 2023. Consent is required before processing sensitive data, and data protection assessments are required for targeted advertising, sale, certain profiling and sensitive data processing.

renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; assessments refreshed on material change
penalties_summary: Attorney General enforcement only, with civil penalties of up to 7,500 US dollars per violation plus recovery of expenses; there is no private right of action.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are organized around notices, consumer rights, sensitive data, data protection assessments and processor contracts. The statute provides a 30-day cure period before enforcement.

scope_summary: Applies to personal data of Utah residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. penalties_summary: Attorney General enforcement only under the state's consumer protection framework; there is no private right of action, and the per-violation maximum is set by that statute.

A 60-day cure period applied through December 31, 2025, after which cure is discretionary; the Secretary of State may set privacy notice standards.

name: New Jersey Data Privacy Act
issuing_body: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs; NJ Attorney General
source_note: Comprehensive state privacy law effective January 2025 with rulemaking authority for the Division of Consumer Affairs
who_must_comply: Businesses that conduct business in New Jersey or target New Jersey residents and meet the applicability thresholds: controlling or processing personal data of at least 100,000 New Jersey consumers excluding payment-transaction-only data, or at least 25,000 consumers while deriving revenue or receiving a benefit from the sale of personal data.
scope_summary: Applies to personal data of New Jersey residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. The Division of Consumer Affairs has rulemaking authority to add detail.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on January 15, 2025. Consent is required for sensitive data, for selling data or targeted advertising involving consumers aged 13 to 16, and controllers must honor universal opt-out mechanisms and complete data protection assessments.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|data inventory|records of processing|data protection assessments|processor contracts (DPAs)|consumer rights request log|opt-out and preference-signal configuration|consent records for sensitive data
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; assessments refreshed on material change
penalties_summary: Attorney General and Division of Consumer Affairs enforcement under the Consumer Fraud Act, which provides penalties of up to 10,000 US dollars for a first violation and 20,000 US dollars for subsequent violations; there is no private right of action.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are organized around notices, consumer rights, sensitive data, data protection assessments and processor contracts. A 30-day cure period applied for the first 18 months after the effective date; controllers must recognize universal opt-out mechanisms.

name: Tennessee Information Protection Act
issuing_body: Tennessee General Assembly; Tennessee Attorney General
source_note: Comprehensive state privacy law effective July 2025; offers an affirmative defense for NIST Privacy Framework alignment
who_must_comply: Businesses that conduct business in Tennessee or target Tennessee residents and meet the applicability thresholds: revenue exceeding 25 million US dollars plus either controlling or processing personal data of at least 175,000 Tennessee consumers, or at least 25,000 consumers while deriving more than 50 percent of gross revenue from the sale of personal data.
scope_summary: Applies to personal data of Tennessee residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Applies only to controllers and processors with more than 25 million US dollars in revenue.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on July 1, 2025. Consent is required for sensitive data, data protection assessments are required for higher-risk processing, and maintaining a NIST Privacy Framework-aligned program provides an affirmative defense.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|data inventory|records of processing|data protection assessments|processor contracts (DPAs)|consumer rights request log|opt-out and preference-signal configuration|consent records for sensitive data
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; assessments refreshed on material change
penalties_summary: Attorney General enforcement only, with civil penalties of up to 7,500 US dollars per violation and treble damages available for willful or knowing violations; there is no private right of action.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are organized around notices, consumer rights, sensitive data, data protection assessments and processor contracts. A 60-day cure period applies, and the statute provides an affirmative defense for controllers and processors that maintain a written privacy program reasonably conforming to the NIST Privacy Framework.

name: Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act
source_note: Comprehensive state privacy law codified at Minn. Stat. ch. 325M, effective July 2025, adding profiling-specific consumer rights
who_must_comply: Businesses that conduct business in Minnesota or target Minnesota residents and meet the applicability thresholds: controlling or processing personal data of at least 100,000 Minnesota consumers excluding payment-transaction-only data, or at least 25,000 consumers while deriving over 25 percent of gross revenue from the sale of personal data.
scope_summary: Applies to personal data of Minnesota residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Codified at Minnesota Statutes chapter 325O; small businesses are largely exempt.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on July 31, 2025. Controllers must maintain a data inventory, and consumers can question the result of profiling in furtherance of a decision with legal or similarly significant effects, review data used, and obtain a list of specific third parties that received their data.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|data inventory|records of processing|data protection assessments|processor contracts (DPAs)|consumer rights request log|opt-out and preference-signal configuration|consent records for sensitive data

penalties_summary: Attorney General enforcement only, with civil penalties of up to 7,500 US dollars per violation; there is no private right of action.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are organized around notices, consumer rights, sensitive data, data protection assessments and processor contracts. A 30-day cure period applied through January 31, 2026; the law also requires a documented data inventory and gives consumers profiling-specific rights.

name: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act
issuing_body: Maryland General Assembly; Maryland Attorney General
source_note: Comprehensive state privacy law effective October 2025 with strict data minimization and sensitive data sale ban
who_must_comply: Businesses that conduct business in Maryland or target Maryland residents and meet the applicability thresholds: controlling or processing personal data of at least 35,000 Maryland consumers excluding payment-transaction-only data, or at least 10,000 consumers while deriving more than 20 percent of gross revenue from the sale of personal data.
scope_summary: Applies to personal data of Maryland residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. This law imposes the strictest data minimization standard among U.S. state privacy laws.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on October 1, 2025. Collection is limited to what is reasonably necessary to provide the specific product or service requested, sale of sensitive data is prohibited, and targeted advertising or sale of data of consumers under 18 is prohibited.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|data inventory|records of processing|data protection assessments|processor contracts (DPAs)|consumer rights request log|opt-out and preference-signal configuration|consent records for sensitive data

penalties_summary: Attorney General enforcement as an unfair or deceptive trade practice, with civil penalties of up to 10,000 US dollars per violation and up to 25,000 US dollars for repeat violations; there is no private right of action.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are organized around notices, consumer rights, sensitive data, data protection assessments and processor contracts. There is no general cure period after the initial transition; obligations include a strict necessity standard for collection and processing.

scope_summary: Applies to personal data of Indiana residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Closely modeled on the Virginia statute.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on January 1, 2026. name: Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act
issuing_body: Rhode Island General Assembly; RI Attorney General
source_note: Comprehensive state privacy law effective January 2026 with notably low applicability thresholds
who_must_comply: Businesses that conduct business in Rhode Island or target Rhode Island residents and meet the applicability thresholds: controlling or processing personal data of at least 35,000 Rhode Island customers, or at least 10,000 customers while deriving more than 20 percent of gross revenue from the sale of personal data.
scope_summary: Applies to personal data of Rhode Island residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Applicability thresholds are among the lowest, and the notice duties are unusually specific.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on January 1, 2026. In addition to standard rights and opt-outs, controllers must name the third parties to which personal data has been or may be sold in the privacy notice, and consent is required for sensitive data.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|data inventory|records of processing|data protection assessments|processor contracts (DPAs)|consumer rights request log|opt-out and preference-signal configuration|consent records for sensitive data

penalties_summary: Attorney General enforcement only, with penalties of up to 10,000 US dollars per intentional disclosure violation as specified in the statute; there is no private right of action.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are organized around notices, consumer rights, sensitive data, data protection assessments and processor contracts. The statute requires controllers that sell personal data or process it for targeted advertising to identify in the privacy notice all third parties to which data has been or may be sold.

name: NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation
issuing_body: New York State Department of Financial Services
source_note: Cybersecurity program, CISO, MFA, and reporting requirements for NYDFS-covered financial entities
who_must_comply: Entities operating under a New York banking, insurance or financial services license or registration, with tiered relief for small covered entities and additional duties for Class A companies.
scope_summary: Covers the covered entity's information systems and nonpublic information, including systems operated by affiliates and third-party service providers.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a written cybersecurity program and policy approved by the board or senior governing body, a qualified CISO reporting at least annually, risk assessments, multi-factor authentication for all remote and privileged access, asset inventories, encryption, incident response and business continuity plans, and a written third-party service provider policy. Cybersecurity events must be reported to the Department within 72 hours and extortion payments within 24 hours, with an annual notice of compliance filed by April 15. Class A companies must obtain independent audits and implement additional controls such as privileged access management and endpoint detection and response.
typical_evidence_artifacts: cybersecurity policy|risk assessment|CISO annual report|asset inventory|MFA configuration evidence|penetration test and vulnerability scan reports|incident reports|annual certification of compliance|vendor due diligence records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual certification, annual penetration testing and at least biannual vulnerability assessments
penalties_summary: Enforcement under New York Banking, Insurance and Financial Services Law, with per-violation penalties and consent orders that have reached multi-million-dollar settlements; each day of non-compliance can be treated as a separate violation.
subordinate_controls_notes: Sections 500.1 to 500.24 cover program, policy, CISO, testing, audit trails, access, application security, risk assessment, personnel, third parties, MFA, retention, monitoring, encryption, incident response and notification.

name: Colorado Automated Decision-Making Technology Act
also_known_as: Colorado AI Act; SB 24-205; SB 26-189; ADMT Act
issuing_body: Colorado General Assembly; Colorado Attorney General
source_note: SB 24-205 (Colorado AI Act) was repealed and reenacted by SB 26-189 as the ADMT Act, effective January 1, 2027
who_must_comply: Developers and deployers of automated decision-making or high-risk artificial intelligence systems that affect Colorado residents in consequential decisions such as employment, lending, housing, insurance, education and health care.
scope_summary: Covers automated decision-making technology used in consequential decisions concerning Colorado consumers, with duties allocated between developers and deployers.
key_obligations_summary: The original Colorado AI Act, SB 24-205, imposed reasonable-care duties to avoid algorithmic discrimination, including impact assessments, risk management programs, consumer notices and disclosures to the Attorney General. It was repealed and reenacted by SB 26-189 as the Automated Decision-Making Technology Act, with an effective date of January 1, 2027, so implementing detail and rulemaking are still developing. Organizations should track the reenacted statute's final obligations before building controls.
typical_evidence_artifacts: AI and ADMT system inventory|impact assessments|risk management program documentation|consumer notices|incident and discrimination reporting records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: unknown pending implementation of the reenacted statute
penalties_summary: Exclusive Attorney General enforcement, historically as a deceptive trade practice under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act with no private right of action; specific penalty amounts under the reenacted ADMT Act are unknown.
subordinate_controls_notes: Duties are split between developers and deployers rather than organized into control families; details depend on the reenacted statute and any rules.

name: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act
source_note: Texas AI governance law effective January 1, 2026 covering prohibited uses, disclosures, sandbox, and AI Council
who_must_comply: Persons developing or deploying artificial intelligence systems in Texas, with specific additional duties for state agencies and for health care and biometric use cases.
scope_summary: Covers AI systems developed, marketed, distributed or deployed in Texas, focused on prohibited intentional uses rather than general risk tiering.
key_obligations_summary: Prohibits developing or deploying AI with intent to unlawfully discriminate, incite self-harm or crime, produce certain unlawful sexual content, or infringe constitutional rights, and restricts government use for social scoring and certain biometric identification. Government agencies must disclose AI interactions with consumers, and health care providers must disclose AI use in treatment. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement with a 60-day cure period, and the law creates a regulatory sandbox and an AI Council, effective January 1, 2026.
typical_evidence_artifacts: AI system inventory|intent and use-case documentation|consumer and patient disclosures|risk assessments|training records|sandbox application where used
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; no fixed reassessment cadence in the statute
penalties_summary: Attorney General enforcement with civil penalties in statutory ranges, reported as 10,000 to 12,000 US dollars per curable violation and 80,000 to 200,000 US dollars per uncurable violation, plus daily penalties for continuing violations; there is no private right of action.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are organized around prohibited intents, disclosure duties, sandbox participation and government-specific restrictions.

name: Sarbanes-Oxley Act
source_note: Financial reporting integrity law driving IT general controls for public companies and IPO candidates
who_must_comply: U.S. public companies, their officers and auditors, plus late-stage private companies preparing for an IPO or acquisition by a public filer.
scope_summary: Covers internal control over financial reporting, including the IT general controls and application controls supporting financially relevant systems.
key_obligations_summary: Requires management assertions on disclosure controls under Section 302 and on internal control over financial reporting under Section 404, with auditor attestation for accelerated filers. In IT terms this drives documented IT general controls over access management, change management, IT operations and program development for in-scope systems. Deficiencies are evaluated and, where material, disclosed as significant deficiencies or material weaknesses.
typical_evidence_artifacts: ITGC narratives and process flows|access provisioning and review records|change tickets and approvals|segregation of duties matrix|control testing workpapers|management assertions|auditor reports
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual, with quarterly evaluation of disclosure controls
penalties_summary: Criminal penalties for knowingly false certifications of up to 5 million US dollars and 20 years imprisonment, plus SEC enforcement, restatements and delisting consequences.
subordinate_controls_notes: No official control catalog; programs typically use the COSO 2013 framework with COBIT-aligned IT general control domains.

name: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and FTC Safeguards Rule
also_known_as: GLBA; FTC Safeguards Rule; 16 CFR Part 314
source_note: Written information security program requirements for non-bank financial institutions under FTC jurisdiction
who_must_comply: Non-bank financial institutions under FTC jurisdiction, including many fintechs, lenders, mortgage brokers, auto dealers, tax preparers and finders, plus banks under parallel interagency rules.
scope_summary: Covers customer information handled by a financial institution, including information received about another institution's customers.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a written information security program with a designated qualified individual, a written risk assessment, and specific safeguards including access controls, data inventory, encryption in transit and at rest, secure development practices, multi-factor authentication, disposal, change management and activity monitoring. Institutions must test controls through continuous monitoring or annual penetration testing plus biannual vulnerability assessments, oversee service providers, maintain an incident response plan, and provide an annual written report to the board. Since 2024 they must notify the FTC within 30 days of discovering a security event involving unencrypted customer information of 500 or more consumers, and GLBA privacy notice rules apply separately.
typical_evidence_artifacts: written information security program|risk assessment|qualified individual designation|penetration test and vulnerability scan reports|MFA evidence|data inventory|vendor oversight records|incident response plan|annual board report|privacy notices
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual penetration test and board report, with vulnerability assessments at least every six months
penalties_summary: FTC civil penalties per violation adjusted annually for inflation, currently exceeding 50,000 US dollars per violation, plus consent orders with multi-year compliance obligations.
subordinate_controls_notes: 16 CFR Part 314 elements: program, qualified individual, risk assessment, eight safeguard categories, testing, personnel, service providers, evaluation, incident response and reporting.

name: Bank Secrecy Act / Anti-Money Laundering
source_note: AML program, KYC, recordkeeping, and suspicious activity reporting obligations for covered financial institutions
who_must_comply: Banks, credit unions, money services businesses, broker-dealers, casinos and other financial institutions defined in the regulations, including many crypto and payments firms registered as MSBs.
scope_summary: Covers financial transactions and customer relationships subject to the Bank Secrecy Act and FinCEN regulations in 31 CFR Chapter X.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a risk-based AML and countering the financing of terrorism program with internal controls, a designated compliance officer, training, independent testing and customer due diligence including beneficial ownership identification. Institutions must file suspicious activity reports, generally within 30 days of detection, currency transaction reports for cash transactions above 10,000 US dollars, and maintain records including funds transfer and travel rule information. Sanctions screening under OFAC rules operates in parallel.
typical_evidence_artifacts: AML program policy|risk assessment|CIP and beneficial ownership records|SAR and CTR filings|independent testing report|training records|sanctions screening logs
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual training and periodic independent testing, commonly annual
penalties_summary: Civil money penalties per violation with substantially higher amounts for willful violations, criminal penalties up to 500,000 US dollars and 10 years imprisonment for willful program violations, and enforcement actions restricting business.
subordinate_controls_notes: Programs are commonly organized around the five pillars: internal controls, compliance officer, training, independent testing and customer due diligence.

name: FINRA Rules
also_known_as: FINRA Rulebook; FINRA 4511 recordkeeping; SEA Rule 17a-4
source_note: Self-regulatory rulebook for US broker-dealers covering supervision, recordkeeping, and communications retention
who_must_comply: FINRA member broker-dealers and their associated persons, plus technology vendors supporting their recordkeeping and communications.
scope_summary: Covers member firms' business activities, supervision, communications, books and records, and customer protection obligations.
key_obligations_summary: Requires written supervisory procedures and a supervisory system, review and approval of communications with the public, and preservation of books and records including electronic communications. SEA Rule 17a-4 permits electronic records preservation using either a write-once read-many format or an audit-trail alternative, with a designated third party or executive access undertaking. Firms must also meet cybersecurity, business continuity and customer identification expectations examined by FINRA.
typical_evidence_artifacts: written supervisory procedures|communications review records|archived electronic communications with retention configuration|audit-trail or WORM attestation|business continuity plan|examination responses
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; retention periods are generally 3 to 6 years depending on record type, with annual supervisory reviews
penalties_summary: FINRA disciplinary sanctions including fines, restitution, suspension, bar or expulsion, alongside SEC enforcement for rule violations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Rulebook organized into conduct, supervision, financial and operational, and trading rules, with recordkeeping requirements in FINRA 4511 and SEA Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4.

name: SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Rules
source_note: Requires public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents and describe risk management and governance
who_must_comply: U.S. public companies and certain foreign private issuers subject to SEC reporting.
scope_summary: Applies to registrants' disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents and of cybersecurity risk management, strategy and governance.
key_obligations_summary: Requires disclosure of a material cybersecurity incident on Form 8-K Item 1.05 generally within four business days of determining materiality, with limited national security delays. Annual reports must describe processes for assessing, identifying and managing cybersecurity risks plus board and management oversight under Regulation S-K Item 106. Foreign private issuers report comparable information on Forms 6-K and 20-F.
typical_evidence_artifacts: incident materiality assessment|Form 8-K Item 1.05 filing|Item 106 disclosure|board minutes|incident response plan|disclosure controls documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; annual disclosure in periodic reports
penalties_summary: SEC enforcement for disclosure failures, including civil penalties, plus securities litigation exposure; amounts are case-specific.
subordinate_controls_notes: Implemented through Regulation S-K Item 106 and Form 8-K Item 1.05 rather than a technical control catalog.

name: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook
also_known_as: FFIEC IT Handbook; FFIEC Information Security Booklet
source_note: Interagency examination guidance used by US banking regulators for IT and information security
who_must_comply: U.S. banks, credit unions and their technology service providers examined by the federal banking agencies.
scope_summary: Covers IT governance, information security, business continuity, outsourcing, development and acquisition, and related examination areas.
key_obligations_summary: Provides examination procedures and expectations that institutions use to structure IT risk management, information security programs, resilience and third-party risk. Technology service providers can be examined directly under the Bank Service Company Act. It is supervisory guidance rather than a regulation, but findings drive mandatory remediation.
typical_evidence_artifacts: information security program|IT risk assessment|business continuity and resilience test results|vendor management documentation|board reporting|examination response and remediation plans
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: examination cycles are typically every 12 to 18 months depending on institution size and risk
penalties_summary: No direct fine; examiners issue matters requiring attention or enforcement actions that can escalate to formal agreements, civil money penalties or restrictions on activities.
subordinate_controls_notes: Booklets covering areas such as information security, business continuity management, outsourcing technology services, architecture and operations, and development and acquisition.

name: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
also_known_as: HIPAA; HIPAA Privacy Rule; HIPAA Security Rule; Breach Notification Rule
issuing_body: US Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
source_note: US health privacy and security regime applying to covered entities and business associates
who_must_comply: Covered entities such as health plans, health care clearinghouses and most health care providers, and business associates including many SaaS vendors that handle protected health information.
scope_summary: Covers protected health information created, received, maintained or transmitted by covered entities and business associates, including electronic PHI.
key_obligations_summary: The Privacy Rule limits uses and disclosures of PHI and grants individual rights of access, amendment and accounting of disclosures. The Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards supported by a risk analysis and risk management process, workforce training, contingency planning and audit controls. The Breach Notification Rule requires notice to affected individuals and HHS, generally within 60 days, and business associate agreements are required before PHI is shared with vendors.
typical_evidence_artifacts: risk analysis|policies and procedures|business associate agreements|workforce training records|access logs and audit controls|encryption evidence|contingency plan and test results|breach risk assessments and notifications
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; risk analysis reviewed at least annually and on material change
penalties_summary: Civil money penalties in four tiers based on culpability, with per-violation minimums and annual caps adjusted for inflation, reaching over 2 million US dollars per year for willful neglect that is not corrected; criminal penalties reach 250,000 US dollars and 10 years imprisonment.
subordinate_controls_notes: Security Rule standards and implementation specifications, some required and some addressable, grouped into administrative, physical and technical safeguards plus organizational requirements.

name: HITECH Act
also_known_as: Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act
issuing_body: US Department of Health and Human Services
source_note: Strengthened HIPAA enforcement, breach notification, and business associate liability
who_must_comply: The same covered entities and business associates as HIPAA, with business associates directly liable for specified requirements.
scope_summary: Covers electronic health information practices, breach notification and enforcement layered onto the HIPAA rules.
key_obligations_summary: Extended direct HIPAA liability to business associates, established the tiered civil money penalty structure and mandatory breach notification, and strengthened enforcement including state attorney general authority. Its 2021 amendment requires HHS to consider an entity's recognized security practices maintained for the prior twelve months when determining penalties and audit outcomes. Implementation is largely through the HIPAA Omnibus Rule.
typical_evidence_artifacts: breach notification records|business associate agreements|recognized security practices documentation|risk analysis|training records|policies
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; recognized security practices evidenced over a trailing 12-month period
penalties_summary: Tiered HIPAA civil money penalties adjusted annually for inflation, plus state attorney general enforcement with statutory damages and attorney fees.
subordinate_controls_notes: No separate control catalog; it modifies HIPAA rules and creates the recognized security practices mitigation pathway.

name: FDA 21 CFR Part 11
also_known_as: Part 11; electronic records and electronic signatures
source_note: Requirements for electronic records and signatures in FDA-regulated environments; foundation of computer system validation
who_must_comply: FDA-regulated organizations and their software suppliers that create, modify, maintain, archive, retrieve or transmit records required by FDA predicate rules in electronic form.
scope_summary: Covers electronic records and electronic signatures used to satisfy FDA predicate rule requirements, in closed and open systems.
key_obligations_summary: Requires validation of systems to ensure accuracy, reliability and consistent intended performance, secure computer-generated time-stamped audit trails, authority checks, and record retention and retrieval throughout the required period. Electronic signatures must be unique, verified, and linked to their records, with certification to the FDA that electronic signatures are legally binding. FDA guidance applies a risk-based approach, with computer software assurance guidance for production and quality system software.
typical_evidence_artifacts: validation plan and reports|requirements and traceability matrix|audit trail configuration and review records|user access and authority checks|electronic signature certification letter|SOPs|change control records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; periodic review and revalidation on significant change
penalties_summary: No fixed fine schedule; FDA actions include Form 483 observations, warning letters, import alerts, consent decrees, product seizure and injunctions.
subordinate_controls_notes: Subparts cover general provisions, electronic records including controls for closed and open systems and audit trails, and electronic signature requirements.

name: FDA Current Good Manufacturing Practice regulations
source_note: Quality system regulations for drug manufacturing; the GxP family also covers GCP and GLP
who_must_comply: Manufacturers, packagers and processors of drugs and related products, and suppliers of systems supporting regulated manufacturing and quality operations.
scope_summary: Covers the manufacturing, processing, packing and holding of drug products, with parallel GxP regimes for clinical (GCP) and laboratory (GLP) activities.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a quality unit with defined responsibilities, written and approved procedures, validated processes and equipment, controlled documentation and records, deviation and change control, and investigation of failures. Data integrity expectations, including attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate records, apply to computerized systems. Inspections verify compliance and findings drive corrective action.
typical_evidence_artifacts: quality manual and SOPs|batch records|validation documentation|deviation and CAPA records|training records|equipment qualification|audit trail reviews
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; annual product quality reviews and periodic inspections
penalties_summary: No fixed fine schedule; FDA actions include Form 483 observations, warning letters, import alerts, seizure, injunction and consent decrees, and adulteration findings can carry criminal exposure.
subordinate_controls_notes: Organized by 21 CFR Part 211 subparts covering organization and personnel, buildings and facilities, equipment, controls, production, laboratory controls and records.

name: 42 CFR Part 2
also_known_as: Part 2; substance use disorder patient records confidentiality
issuing_body: US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
source_note: Heightened confidentiality rules for substance use disorder treatment records, aligned toward HIPAA by the CARES Act
who_must_comply: Federally assisted substance use disorder treatment programs, and lawful holders of Part 2 records including many health technology vendors.
scope_summary: Covers records of the identity, diagnosis, prognosis or treatment of any patient created by a federally assisted substance use disorder program.
key_obligations_summary: Requires written patient consent for use and disclosure of Part 2 records, with narrow exceptions such as medical emergencies, audits and qualified service organization arrangements. The 2024 final rule aligns Part 2 more closely with HIPAA, permitting a single consent for treatment, payment and health care operations, applying HIPAA breach notification and enforcement, and requiring notices and safeguards against use in legal proceedings. Compliance with the 2024 rule is required by February 16, 2026.
typical_evidence_artifacts: patient consent forms|qualified service organization agreements|notice to patients|disclosure accounting|redisclosure notices|breach notifications|policies and training records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; consents managed per patient and revisited on change
penalties_summary: Enforcement aligned with HIPAA under the 2024 rule, exposing violations to HIPAA civil money penalties and, for certain disclosures, criminal penalties.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control families; obligations are structured around consent, redisclosure limits, security of records and prohibitions on use in proceedings.

name: EU Medical Device Regulation
source_note: Conformity assessment and post-market requirements for medical devices including software as a medical device
who_must_comply: Manufacturers, authorized representatives, importers and distributors of medical devices placed on the EU market, including standalone software qualifying as a medical device.
scope_summary: Covers medical devices and accessories placed on the EU market, classified as Class I, IIa, IIb or III based on risk.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a quality management system, technical documentation, clinical evaluation, risk management and, for most classes, conformity assessment involving a notified body before CE marking. Manufacturers must register devices and economic operators in EUDAMED, assign Unique Device Identifiers, appoint a person responsible for regulatory compliance, and operate post-market surveillance and vigilance including incident reporting. Software as a medical device must also meet cybersecurity and IEC 62304-style lifecycle expectations reflected in guidance.
typical_evidence_artifacts: technical documentation|clinical evaluation report|risk management file|QMS records (ISO 13485)|EU declaration of conformity and CE certificate|post-market surveillance plan and reports|vigilance reports|UDI and EUDAMED registrations
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; notified body surveillance audits annually and certificate renewal typically every 5 years
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by member states and must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive; regulators can also suspend or withdraw devices from the market.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured by device classification rules, general safety and performance requirements in Annex I, and conformity assessment routes in the annexes.

name: EU In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation
source_note: Conformity assessment requirements for in vitro diagnostic medical devices
who_must_comply: Manufacturers and other economic operators placing in vitro diagnostic medical devices, including diagnostic software and algorithms, on the EU market.
scope_summary: Covers in vitro diagnostic medical devices classified as Class A, B, C or D based on risk to individuals and public health.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a quality management system, technical documentation, performance evaluation including scientific validity and clinical performance, and notified body conformity assessment for most classes before CE marking. Manufacturers must register in EUDAMED, assign UDIs, appoint a person responsible for regulatory compliance and conduct post-market performance follow-up and vigilance reporting. Transitional provisions extended deadlines for legacy devices depending on class.
typical_evidence_artifacts: technical documentation|performance evaluation report|risk management file|QMS records (ISO 13485)|EU declaration of conformity and CE certificate|post-market performance follow-up plan|vigilance reports|UDI and EUDAMED registrations
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; notified body surveillance audits annually and certificate renewal typically every 5 years
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by member states and must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, alongside market withdrawal powers.
subordinate_controls_notes: Classification rules A to D, general safety and performance requirements, and annex-based conformity assessment routes.

name: European Health Data Space Regulation
source_note: Adopted 11 February 2025; in force 26 March 2025 with phased application from 2027 onward
who_must_comply: Health care providers, health data holders, EHR system manufacturers and secondary users of electronic health data in the EU, including health technology vendors.
scope_summary: Covers primary use of electronic health data for care and secondary use for research, innovation, policy and regulatory purposes, plus EHR system requirements.
key_obligations_summary: Establishes rights for individuals to access and control their electronic health data, obligations for data holders to make defined categories available for secondary use through health data access bodies, and essential requirements for EHR systems including interoperability and logging. Manufacturers of EHR systems must issue declarations of conformity and meet European interoperability and security requirements. The regulation entered into force in March 2025 with obligations phasing in from 2027 onward.
typical_evidence_artifacts: data holder inventories|data access applications and permits|interoperability documentation|EHR system declaration of conformity|logging and access records|patient information notices
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; phased application dates from 2027 through 2031
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by member states, with the regulation also providing for periodic penalty payments in respect of certain secondary-use obligations; amounts vary nationally.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured by chapters on primary use, EHR systems, secondary use and governance rather than a technical control catalog.

name: General Data Protection Regulation
issuing_body: European Union; enforced by national DPAs and the EDPB
source_note: EU-wide personal data protection regulation with extraterritorial reach
who_must_comply: Any organization established in the EU or EEA that processes personal data, and non-EU organizations offering goods or services to, or monitoring the behavior of, people in the EU or EEA.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal data of individuals in the EU and EEA by controllers and processors, including many non-EU companies with no local entity.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a lawful basis for processing, transparency notices, and support for data subject rights including access, erasure, rectification, portability and objection. Controllers must maintain records of processing, apply data protection by design and by default, sign Article 28 contracts with processors, run DPIAs for high-risk processing and notify personal data breaches to the supervisory authority within 72 hours. Transfers outside the EEA require an adequacy decision, Standard Contractual Clauses or another Chapter V mechanism, and some organizations must appoint a DPO or EU representative.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|records of processing (RoPA)|DPIA|DPA|SCCs|transfer impact assessment|consent records|breach register|training records|subprocessor list
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; DPIAs and RoPA reviewed on material change
penalties_summary: Administrative fines up to 20 million euro or 4 percent of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for the most serious infringements; a lower tier applies up to 10 million euro or 2 percent.
subordinate_controls_notes: No control catalog; obligations are structured by chapters covering principles, rights, controller and processor duties, transfers, supervisory authorities and remedies.

name: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018
source_note: Post-Brexit UK data protection regime; the DPA 2018 supplements the retained UK GDPR
who_must_comply: Organizations established in the UK that process personal data, and non-UK organizations offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in the UK.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of UK personal data by controllers and processors, with the Data Protection Act 2018 supplementing the retained UK GDPR and covering law enforcement and intelligence processing.
key_obligations_summary: Mirrors GDPR requirements for lawful basis, transparency, data subject rights, records of processing, DPIAs and 72-hour breach reporting to the ICO. UK international transfers use UK adequacy regulations, the International Data Transfer Agreement or the UK Addendum to the EU SCCs. Certain organizations must pay the ICO data protection fee and may need a UK representative.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|records of processing|DPIA|DPA|IDTA or UK Addendum|transfer risk assessment|breach register|ICO fee registration
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; ICO registration fee paid annually
penalties_summary: Fines up to 17.5 million pounds or 4 percent of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for the most serious infringements.
subordinate_controls_notes: Follows the UK GDPR article structure plus DPA 2018 parts covering exemptions, law enforcement and intelligence services processing.

name: ePrivacy Directive
source_note: Rules on cookies, terminal equipment access, and electronic marketing, implemented by national laws
who_must_comply: Operators of websites, apps and electronic communications services targeting users in EU member states, plus direct marketers using electronic channels.
scope_summary: Applies to storing or accessing information on users' terminal equipment, such as cookies and similar technologies, and to electronic direct marketing and confidentiality of communications, as implemented in each member state's national law.
key_obligations_summary: Requires informed consent before non-essential cookies or similar technologies are used, with strictly necessary and communications-transmission exemptions. Electronic direct marketing generally requires prior consent, subject to a limited soft opt-in for existing customers under national implementations. Because it is a directive, exact requirements and enforcement depend on national transpositions and regulators.
typical_evidence_artifacts: cookie banner and consent records|cookie policy|tracker inventory|consent management platform logs|marketing consent records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; consent typically refreshed periodically per national guidance
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by national implementing laws and vary by member state; GDPR fines can also apply where consent failures involve personal data.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured as directive articles on confidentiality, terminal equipment access and unsolicited communications rather than a control catalog.

name: Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations
source_note: UK implementation of ePrivacy covering cookies, electronic marketing, and communications security
who_must_comply: Organizations placing cookies or similar technologies on UK users' devices and those sending electronic marketing to UK recipients.
scope_summary: Applies to cookies and similar technologies, unsolicited electronic marketing by email, SMS, phone and fax, and security and confidentiality of public electronic communications services in the UK.
key_obligations_summary: Requires clear information and consent for non-essential cookies, with strictly necessary exemptions. Electronic marketing to individuals generally requires consent, with a soft opt-in available for existing customers on similar products with a clear opt-out. The ICO enforces PECR separately from the UK GDPR.
typical_evidence_artifacts: cookie policy|consent records|tracker inventory|marketing suppression lists|consent management platform logs
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; consent refreshed periodically per ICO guidance
penalties_summary: ICO monetary penalties of up to 500,000 pounds under PECR, alongside possible UK GDPR fines where personal data is involved.
subordinate_controls_notes: Regulation-based obligations covering cookies, direct marketing channels and communications security rather than a control catalog.

name: EU Standard Contractual Clauses
source_note: Approved transfer mechanism for personal data exports from the EEA to third countries
who_must_comply: Any controller or processor exporting personal data from the EEA to a third country without an adequacy decision, including EEA customers' non-EEA vendors.
scope_summary: Applies to the specific transfer relationships covered by the chosen module: controller to controller, controller to processor, processor to processor or processor to controller.
key_obligations_summary: Parties execute the Commission-approved clauses in the applicable module, complete the annexes describing the transfer, security measures and subprocessors, and perform a transfer impact assessment considering third-country law. Supplementary measures may be required where local law undermines the clauses. The clauses are contractual and cannot be materially altered.
typical_evidence_artifacts: executed SCCs|transfer impact assessment|Annex I to III documentation|subprocessor list|technical and organizational measures description
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: reviewed on material change; transfer assessments typically refreshed annually
penalties_summary: No separate penalty; unlawful transfers are enforced as GDPR infringements with fines up to 20 million euro or 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover.
subordinate_controls_notes: Four modules with annexes covering transfer details, technical and organizational measures and subprocessors.

name: NIS2 Directive
source_note: Cyber risk management, governance, and incident reporting duties for essential and important entities and their suppliers
who_must_comply: Medium and large entities in listed critical and important sectors in the EU, plus suppliers that receive flowed-down requirements.
scope_summary: Applies to essential and important entities in covered sectors established or offering services in the EU, as transposed by each member state.
key_obligations_summary: Requires risk management measures covering policies, incident handling, business continuity, supply chain security, vulnerability handling, cryptography and access control. Incident reporting follows a staged timeline with early warning within 24 hours and a notification within 72 hours to the national CSIRT or authority. Management bodies carry approval and training responsibilities, and national transposition determines registration and supervision details.
typical_evidence_artifacts: risk assessment|security policies|incident reports|business continuity plan|supplier security clauses|training records|management approval evidence
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; supervisory audits vary by member state
penalties_summary: For essential entities, administrative fines up to 10 million euro or 2 percent of total worldwide annual turnover; for important entities, up to 7 million euro or 1.4 percent, plus possible management liability.
subordinate_controls_notes: Article 21 lists ten baseline risk-management measure categories; member states may add national control frameworks.

name: EU Cyber Resilience Act
source_note: Horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements; reporting duties from September 2026, full application December 2027
who_must_comply: Manufacturers, importers and distributors placing products with digital elements, including software, on the EU market.
scope_summary: Applies to hardware and software products with digital elements made available on the EU market, with heightened rules for important and critical categories.
key_obligations_summary: Requires security by design and by default, a conformity assessment appropriate to the product class, CE marking, and technical documentation including a software bill of materials. Manufacturers must handle vulnerabilities for the support period and report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents to ENISA and national authorities within defined deadlines. Main obligations apply from December 2027, with reporting duties from September 2026.
typical_evidence_artifacts: technical documentation|SBOM|risk assessment|conformity assessment records|EU declaration of conformity|vulnerability handling policy|incident reports
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous during the support period; reassessment on substantial modification
penalties_summary: Administrative fines up to 15 million euro or 2.5 percent of worldwide annual turnover for the most serious breaches, with lower tiers for other obligations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Essential cybersecurity requirements and vulnerability handling requirements in the annexes, with product classes determining conformity assessment routes.

name: EU Artificial Intelligence Act
source_note: Risk-tiered obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems and general-purpose AI models
who_must_comply: Providers, deployers, importers and distributors of AI systems placed on the EU market or whose output is used in the EU, plus providers of general-purpose AI models.
scope_summary: Applies by risk tier: prohibited practices, high-risk systems listed in the annexes, limited-risk systems with transparency duties, and general-purpose AI models with separate provider obligations.
key_obligations_summary: Prohibits specified practices such as social scoring and certain biometric categorization, and imposes on high-risk systems a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy and robustness, conformity assessment, CE marking and post-market monitoring. Deployers of high-risk systems have duties including human oversight, input data relevance, log retention and, for some public bodies, fundamental rights impact assessments. Obligations phase in from February 2025 for prohibitions and AI literacy, August 2025 for general-purpose AI models and governance, and August 2026 and 2027 for most high-risk requirements.
typical_evidence_artifacts: AI system inventory and role determination|risk classification records|technical documentation|data governance records|conformity assessment and CE marking|post-market monitoring plan|incident reports|instructions for use
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; documentation updated on substantial modification and through post-market monitoring
penalties_summary: Administrative fines up to 35 million euro or 7 percent of total worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices, up to 15 million euro or 3 percent for most other obligations including general-purpose AI model duties, and up to 7.5 million euro or 1 percent for supplying incorrect information.
subordinate_controls_notes: Risk tiers plus Chapter III requirements for high-risk systems, Chapter V for general-purpose AI models, and Annex III listing high-risk use cases.

name: Digital Operational Resilience Act
source_note: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, and third-party oversight for EU financial entities
who_must_comply: EU financial entities such as banks, insurers, investment firms and crypto-asset service providers, plus ICT third-party providers serving them.
scope_summary: Applies to in-scope EU financial entities and, through designation, to critical ICT third-party service providers.
key_obligations_summary: Requires an ICT risk management framework, classification and reporting of major ICT-related incidents, digital operational resilience testing including threat-led penetration testing for larger entities, and management of ICT third-party risk with a register of information and mandatory contractual terms. Financial entities must maintain exit strategies and concentration risk analysis for critical providers. Critical ICT providers are subject to direct EU oversight.
typical_evidence_artifacts: ICT risk management framework|register of information|incident classification and reports|resilience testing reports|contractual clauses|exit plans
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; threat-led penetration testing at least every 3 years for in-scope entities
penalties_summary: Supervisory measures and member-state penalties for financial entities; critical ICT third-party providers face periodic penalty payments of up to 1 percent of average daily worldwide turnover.
subordinate_controls_notes: Requirements are grouped into ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party risk and information sharing pillars, detailed by regulatory technical standards.

name: Payment Services Directive 2
source_note: Payment services rules including strong customer authentication and access to accounts
who_must_comply: Payment service providers in the EU, including banks, payment institutions, e-money institutions and third-party providers using account access APIs.
scope_summary: Applies to payment services provided in the EU, including account information and payment initiation services and the security of electronic payments.
key_obligations_summary: Requires authorization or registration as a payment service provider, strong customer authentication for most electronic payments with defined exemptions, secure communication with account servicing providers, and incident and fraud reporting. Regulatory technical standards specify SCA and secure communication requirements. National competent authorities supervise compliance.
typical_evidence_artifacts: authorization or registration records|SCA implementation documentation|API and interface documentation|fraud reporting|incident reports|security policies
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous with periodic supervisory review and annual fraud reporting
penalties_summary: Member-state administrative penalties set in national law; supervisory measures can include restrictions or withdrawal of authorization.
subordinate_controls_notes: Core obligations plus Commission Delegated Regulation 2018/389 regulatory technical standards on strong customer authentication and common and secure communication.

name: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II
source_note: EU investment services regime including recordkeeping, communications retention, and conduct rules
who_must_comply: Investment firms, credit institutions providing investment services, and trading venues operating in the EU, plus vendors supporting their recordkeeping.
scope_summary: Covers investment services and activities in financial instruments, including client communications, order handling, trading and reporting.
key_obligations_summary: Requires recording and retention of telephone conversations and electronic communications relating to orders, generally for five years and up to seven years if requested by a competent authority. Firms must meet best execution, product governance, suitability and appropriateness, transaction reporting and cost and charges disclosure requirements. National competent authorities supervise compliance under the directive as transposed.
typical_evidence_artifacts: communications recording and archives|order and transaction records|best execution policy and monitoring reports|product governance documentation|suitability assessments|retention configuration evidence
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; record retention generally 5 years, extendable to 7 years on request
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by member states, with the directive requiring minimum maximum administrative fines including at least 5 million euro for legal persons in specified cases; national laws frequently set higher amounts.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations flow from the directive, MiFIR and delegated regulations rather than a control catalog.

name: Basel III
also_known_as: Basel III framework; Basel Committee capital and liquidity standards
issuing_body: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, BIS
source_note: International bank capital, leverage, and liquidity standards implemented through national regulation
who_must_comply: Internationally active banks, as implemented by national banking regulators; not directly applicable to non-bank technology companies.
scope_summary: Covers bank regulatory capital, leverage, liquidity and risk-weighted asset calculation, including operational risk capital.
key_obligations_summary: Sets minimum risk-based capital and leverage ratios, liquidity coverage and net stable funding requirements, and buffers such as the countercyclical and capital conservation buffers. The finalized reforms revise credit, market and operational risk measurement, including a standardized operational risk approach that uses loss history. Requirements bind only as implemented in national law and supervisory rules.
typical_evidence_artifacts: regulatory capital calculations|risk-weighted asset models and documentation|liquidity reporting|ICAAP and stress test results|supervisory reporting returns|operational loss data
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; regulatory reporting quarterly with annual supervisory review
penalties_summary: No penalty from the Basel Committee, which sets standards; national regulators impose capital add-ons, restrictions on distributions and enforcement actions.
subordinate_controls_notes: Pillar 1 minimum requirements, Pillar 2 supervisory review and Pillar 3 disclosure, with separate credit, market, operational and liquidity components.

name: Digital Services Act
source_note: Obligations for online intermediaries and platforms on notice-and-action, transparency, and systemic risk
who_must_comply: Providers of intermediary services offered to users in the EU, including hosting services, online platforms, marketplaces and designated very large online platforms and search engines.
scope_summary: Applies by service tier, with cumulative duties for intermediaries, hosting providers, online platforms and very large platforms or search engines with over 45 million monthly EU users.
key_obligations_summary: Requires transparent terms, notice and action mechanisms, statements of reasons for content decisions, internal complaint handling and out-of-court dispute settlement, plus points of contact and legal representatives. Online platforms face additional duties on trader traceability, advertising transparency, protection of minors and dark pattern prohibitions, while designated very large platforms must conduct systemic risk assessments, independent audits and data access for researchers. Micro and small enterprises are exempt from several platform-specific obligations.
typical_evidence_artifacts: terms of service|notice and action workflow records|statements of reasons and DSA transparency database submissions|transparency reports|systemic risk assessment and audit reports for designated services|advertising repository
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual transparency reporting; annual independent audits for very large platforms
penalties_summary: Fines up to 6 percent of annual worldwide turnover for infringements, with periodic penalty payments and, for very large services, supervisory fees and Commission enforcement.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are layered by service category rather than organized into control families.

name: Digital Markets Act
source_note: Ex ante obligations for designated gatekeeper core platform services
who_must_comply: Undertakings designated by the European Commission as gatekeepers operating core platform services, and, indirectly, business users that rely on them.
scope_summary: Covers designated core platform services such as app stores, search engines, social networks, messaging, operating systems and advertising services meeting quantitative thresholds.
key_obligations_summary: Imposes ex ante obligations on gatekeepers including interoperability, data portability, restrictions on self-preferencing and on combining personal data across services without consent, and fair access terms for business users. Gatekeepers must notify designation-relevant thresholds, submit compliance reports and inform the Commission of intended acquisitions. Most companies are affected as business users rather than as regulated gatekeepers.
typical_evidence_artifacts: designation notification|annual compliance report|data portability and interoperability documentation|consent records for data combination|contractual terms for business users
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual compliance reporting
penalties_summary: Fines up to 10 percent of total worldwide turnover, rising to 20 percent for repeated infringements, plus periodic penalty payments and structural remedies for systematic non-compliance.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are set out in Articles 5, 6 and 7 for designated gatekeepers rather than as a control catalog.

name: EU Data Act
source_note: Rules on access to connected-product data, cloud switching, and unfair data contract terms
who_must_comply: Manufacturers and providers of connected products and related services in the EU, data holders, and providers of data processing services such as cloud and edge providers.
scope_summary: Covers access to and sharing of data generated by connected products and related services, cloud switching, unfair data-sharing contract terms and international access safeguards.
key_obligations_summary: Requires connected products and related services to be designed so that data is accessible to users, and data holders to share data with users and, on request, with third parties on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms. Cloud and edge providers must remove switching charges on the statutory timeline, provide contractual switching terms with defined transition periods, and support functional equivalence or export of exportable data. It also invalidates unfair unilaterally imposed data contract terms and adds safeguards against unlawful third-country access. Most obligations apply from 12 September 2025.
typical_evidence_artifacts: data access documentation|standard contractual terms for data sharing|switching and exit procedures|charge removal evidence|contract templates|international transfer safeguards
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; contract reviews on renewal and on regulatory milestones
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by member states and must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive; GDPR fine levels apply where personal data obligations overlap.
subordinate_controls_notes: Chapters cover business-to-consumer and business-to-business data sharing, unfair terms, public body access, cloud switching and interoperability.

name: European Accessibility Act
source_note: Accessibility requirements for products and services including e-commerce and consumer digital services
who_must_comply: Economic operators placing in-scope products or providing in-scope services on the EU market, including e-commerce, e-books, banking services, transport and telecom services.
scope_summary: Covers listed products and services supplied to consumers in the EU, with microenterprise exemptions for services and disproportionate burden assessments.
key_obligations_summary: Requires in-scope products and services to meet functional accessibility requirements, documented in technical documentation or an accessibility statement. Conformity is presumed where harmonized standards such as EN 301 549 are met. Requirements apply from 28 June 2025, with transitional periods for some services and self-service terminals, and enforcement is by designated national authorities.
typical_evidence_artifacts: accessibility statement|technical documentation|EN 301 549 conformance evidence|disproportionate burden assessment|test results|remediation plan
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; documentation updated on material change
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by each member state and must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive; amounts vary by country.
