subordinate_controls_notes: Functional accessibility requirements in the annexes, with EN 301 549 providing the harmonized technical criteria that reference WCAG.

name: Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive
source_note: Mandatory sustainability reporting under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards
who_must_comply: Large EU companies and listed SMEs meeting size thresholds, plus certain non-EU parent companies with substantial EU turnover and an EU subsidiary or branch.
scope_summary: Covers sustainability reporting on environmental, social and governance matters using a double materiality assessment across the company's own operations and value chain.
key_obligations_summary: Requires reporting under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards in the management report, tagged in a digital format, and subject to limited assurance by an auditor or independent assurance provider. Companies must perform a double materiality assessment covering impacts, risks and opportunities. Application is phased, and the 2025 stop-the-clock directive postponed reporting for the second and third waves by two years while scope simplification is negotiated.
typical_evidence_artifacts: double materiality assessment|ESRS disclosures in the management report|value chain data collection records|assurance report|digital tagging (ESEF) files|internal control documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: Penalties are set by member states and vary, and can include administrative fines, public statements and, in some jurisdictions, director liability.
subordinate_controls_notes: European Sustainability Reporting Standards comprising cross-cutting standards plus environmental, social and governance topical standards.

name: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
issuing_body: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
source_note: Canadian federal private-sector privacy law; some provinces have substantially similar regimes
who_must_comply: Private-sector organizations that collect, use or disclose personal information in the course of commercial activities in Canada, or that transfer such data across provincial or national borders.
scope_summary: Applies to commercial personal information handling in Canada, except in provinces with substantially similar private-sector laws such as Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia for intra-provincial activity.
key_obligations_summary: Requires compliance with ten fair information principles including accountability, identifying purposes, consent, limiting use and retention, safeguards and openness. Organizations must appoint a privacy officer, respond to access requests, and report breaches of security safeguards involving real risk of significant harm to the Privacy Commissioner and affected individuals. Accountability is retained when personal information is transferred to third-party processors, including across borders.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy policy|consent records|access request log|breach records and reports|vendor contracts|safeguards documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; program review commonly annual
penalties_summary: Fines up to 100,000 Canadian dollars per offence for specified violations such as obstructing an investigation or breach-reporting failures; the Commissioner may also publish findings and seek Federal Court orders.
subordinate_controls_notes: Built on the ten fair information principles in Schedule 1 rather than a technical control catalog.

name: Quebec Law 25
also_known_as: Law 25; Bill 64; Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector
issuing_body: Commission d'acces a l'information du Quebec
source_note: Quebec private-sector privacy regime modernized by Law 25, including portability and privacy-by-default duties
who_must_comply: Private-sector enterprises that collect, hold, use or communicate personal information of people in Quebec, and public bodies under parallel rules.
scope_summary: Applies to personal information handled by enterprises carrying on business in Quebec, including data processed outside Quebec on their behalf.
key_obligations_summary: Requires designation of a person in charge of protection of personal information, privacy impact assessments for information system projects and cross-border transfers, and confidentiality by default for technology products and services. Enterprises must report confidentiality incidents presenting a risk of serious injury to the Commission d'acces a l'information and affected individuals, and honor rights including access, correction, de-indexing and, since 2024, data portability. Consent rules are strict, with specific requirements for sensitive information and for profiling or location technologies.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy policy|privacy impact assessments|incident register|consent records|transfer assessments|governance policies
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; assessments per project and on material change
penalties_summary: Administrative monetary penalties up to 10 million Canadian dollars or 2 percent of worldwide turnover, and penal fines up to 25 million Canadian dollars or 4 percent of worldwide turnover, with a private right of action for punitive damages.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are structured by statutory sections covering governance, consent, rights, incidents and transfers.

name: Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation
source_note: Consent, identification, and unsubscribe requirements for commercial electronic messages
who_must_comply: Any organization sending commercial electronic messages to recipients in Canada, or installing computer programs on Canadian users' devices.
scope_summary: Applies to commercial electronic messages such as email and SMS sent to or accessed in Canada, and to computer program installation, regardless of sender location.
key_obligations_summary: Requires express or implied consent before sending commercial electronic messages, clear sender identification and contact information, and a working unsubscribe mechanism honored within ten business days. Consent records must be retained and proof of consent rests with the sender. Separate rules govern consent for installing computer programs.
typical_evidence_artifacts: consent records|suppression list|message templates with identification and unsubscribe|complaint handling records|marketing policy
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; implied consent generally expires after defined periods
penalties_summary: Administrative monetary penalties up to 1 million Canadian dollars per violation for individuals and 10 million Canadian dollars per violation for organizations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Requirements are organized around consent, identification and unsubscribe rather than control families.

name: Lei Geral de Protecao de Dados
also_known_as: LGPD; Brazilian General Data Protection Law; Lei 13.709/2018
issuing_body: Autoridade Nacional de Protecao de Dados (ANPD)
source_note: Brazil's GDPR-inspired data protection law enforced by the ANPD
who_must_comply: Organizations that process personal data in Brazil, offer goods or services in Brazil, or process data collected in Brazil, regardless of where they are based.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal data of individuals in Brazil by controllers and operators, in physical or digital form, with limited exceptions such as purely personal or journalistic use.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a legal basis from the statutory list, transparency, and support for data subject rights including confirmation, access, correction, anonymization, portability and deletion. Controllers must appoint a data protection officer, keep records of processing, adopt security and governance measures, and report security incidents to the ANPD and affected individuals within a deadline set by regulation. International transfers require adequacy, contractual instruments approved by the ANPD or another statutory basis.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|records of processing|legitimate interest assessment|DPIA (RIPD)|DPO appointment|incident reports|international transfer contracts
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; assessments reviewed on material change
penalties_summary: Administrative fines up to 2 percent of Brazilian group revenue for the prior fiscal year, capped at 50 million Brazilian reais per infringement, plus daily fines, publication and processing restrictions.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured by statutory chapters covering legal bases, rights, controller and operator duties, security, transfers and enforcement.

name: Australia Privacy Act 1988
also_known_as: Australian Privacy Principles; APPs; Privacy Act
issuing_body: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
source_note: Australian federal privacy regime built on the 13 Australian Privacy Principles; subject to ongoing reform
who_must_comply: Australian government agencies and private-sector organizations with annual turnover above 3 million Australian dollars, plus smaller entities in categories such as health service providers and those trading in personal information.
scope_summary: Applies to handling of personal information by APP entities, including overseas entities carrying on business in Australia and collecting Australian personal information.
key_obligations_summary: Requires compliance with the thirteen Australian Privacy Principles covering open and transparent management, collection, use and disclosure, direct marketing, cross-border disclosure, data quality, security, access and correction. Entities must have a clearly expressed and up-to-date privacy policy and take reasonable steps to protect and destroy or de-identify information. Eligible data breaches must be assessed and notified to the OAIC and affected individuals under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy policy|APP compliance assessment|collection notices|breach assessment and notifications|overseas disclosure records|security controls documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; policy and program review commonly annual
penalties_summary: Civil penalties for serious or repeated interferences with privacy of up to the greater of 50 million Australian dollars, three times the benefit obtained, or 30 percent of adjusted turnover in the relevant period.
subordinate_controls_notes: Thirteen Australian Privacy Principles, supported by the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme and OAIC guidance.

name: New Zealand Privacy Act 2020
also_known_as: NZ Privacy Act; Information Privacy Principles
issuing_body: Office of the Privacy Commissioner (New Zealand)
source_note: New Zealand privacy regime with information privacy principles and mandatory breach notification
who_must_comply: Any agency, including overseas businesses carrying on business in New Zealand, that handles personal information about identifiable individuals.
scope_summary: Applies to collection, use, disclosure, storage and access of personal information by agencies in New Zealand, including foreign entities operating there.
key_obligations_summary: Requires compliance with the information privacy principles covering purpose, source, collection notice, security, access, correction, accuracy, retention, use, disclosure, unique identifiers and cross-border disclosure. Privacy breaches causing or likely to cause serious harm must be notified to the Privacy Commissioner and affected individuals as soon as practicable. Disclosures to overseas recipients require comparable safeguards under principle 12.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy statement|breach assessment and notification records|access request log|overseas disclosure safeguards|security documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; program review commonly annual
penalties_summary: Fines up to 10,000 New Zealand dollars for specified offences such as failing to notify a notifiable breach; the Human Rights Review Tribunal can award damages for interference with privacy.
subordinate_controls_notes: Thirteen information privacy principles plus breach notification duties.

name: Personal Information Protection Law of China
issuing_body: National People's Congress; Cyberspace Administration of China
source_note: China's comprehensive personal information law including cross-border transfer mechanisms; official NPC text in Chinese
who_must_comply: Organizations handling personal information of individuals in China, including foreign entities that process such data to provide products or services to them or to analyze their behavior.
scope_summary: Applies to personal information handling activities within China and, extraterritorially, to specified processing of Chinese residents' data outside China.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a lawful basis, usually separate consent for sensitive personal information, cross-border transfers and disclosure to third parties, plus transparency and individual rights including access, correction, deletion and portability. Handlers must conduct personal information protection impact assessments, keep records and, above thresholds, appoint a protection officer and a domestic representative. Cross-border transfers require a CAC security assessment, CAC standard contract filing or certification, subject to current CAC exemption rules.
typical_evidence_artifacts: consent records|privacy notice|personal information protection impact assessment|cross-border transfer filing or assessment|processing records|security measures documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; compliance audits required periodically under CAC rules
penalties_summary: Fines up to 50 million Chinese yuan or 5 percent of prior-year turnover for serious violations, plus business suspension, license revocation and personal liability for responsible individuals.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured by statutory chapters on handling rules, sensitive data, cross-border provision, individual rights and handler obligations.

name: Cybersecurity Law of China
issuing_body: National People's Congress; Cyberspace Administration of China
source_note: Foundational Chinese cybersecurity statute covering network operators, MLPS, and data localization; official CAC text in Chinese
who_must_comply: Network operators in China, including most companies operating IT systems there, and operators of critical information infrastructure.
scope_summary: Applies to construction, operation, maintenance and use of networks in mainland China, with heightened duties for critical information infrastructure operators.
key_obligations_summary: Requires tiered network security protection under the Multi-Level Protection Scheme, real-name registration for certain services, incident response and reporting, and retention of network logs for at least six months. Critical information infrastructure operators face procurement security reviews, annual assessments and data localization for personal information and important data. Compliance frequently requires in-country hosting and Chinese-language documentation.
typical_evidence_artifacts: MLPS grading and filing records|security policies|log retention evidence|incident reports|assessment reports|localization architecture documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; annual assessments for critical information infrastructure
penalties_summary: Fines on entities commonly up to 1 million Chinese yuan for serious violations, with additional fines on responsible individuals, service suspension and license revocation.
subordinate_controls_notes: Implemented largely through the Multi-Level Protection Scheme grades and supporting national standards.

name: Data Security Law of China
source_note: Data classification, important data, and cross-border data provision rules for activities in China; official NPC text in Chinese
who_must_comply: Organizations carrying out data processing activities in China, and in some cases outside China where activities harm Chinese national security or public interest.
scope_summary: Applies to all data, not only personal information, with heightened duties for important data and national core data.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a data classification and protection system, risk assessments for important data handlers with reports to regulators, and security management responsibilities across the data lifecycle. Cross-border provision of important data requires security assessment, and providing data to foreign law enforcement requires Chinese government approval. Sector regulators define important data catalogs.
typical_evidence_artifacts: data classification inventory|important data risk assessment reports|security management policies|cross-border assessment filings|incident records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; risk assessments at least annually for important data handlers
penalties_summary: Fines up to 10 million Chinese yuan for the most serious violations such as unlawful provision of national core data, plus business suspension and license revocation.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured around data classification tiers, including important data and national core data, with sector catalogs.

name: Personal Data Protection Act (Singapore)
source_note: Singapore consent, purpose limitation, accountability, and breach notification regime
who_must_comply: Private-sector organizations that collect, use or disclose personal data in Singapore, including foreign organizations with Singapore data processing.
scope_summary: Applies to personal data of individuals handled by organizations in Singapore, excluding public agencies and, for most obligations, employees acting for their organization.
key_obligations_summary: Requires consent or an applicable exception, notification of purposes, and compliance with obligations covering accuracy, protection, retention limitation, access and correction, and transfer limitation. Organizations must appoint a Data Protection Officer and register the contact details, and must notify the PDPC and affected individuals of notifiable data breaches, generally within three calendar days of assessment. Do Not Call provisions apply to marketing messages to Singapore telephone numbers.
typical_evidence_artifacts: data protection policy|DPO appointment|consent and notification records|breach assessment and notification|transfer contracts|Do Not Call screening records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; policy review commonly annual
penalties_summary: Financial penalties up to 10 percent of annual turnover in Singapore or 1 million Singapore dollars, whichever is higher, for data protection breaches.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are grouped into consent, notification, purpose limitation, accuracy, protection, retention, transfer, access and accountability duties.

name: Personal Data Protection Act (Thailand)
source_note: Thailand's GDPR-influenced data protection law enforced by the Thai PDPC; regulator site blocks automated requests, confirm content manually
who_must_comply: Data controllers and processors handling personal data of people in Thailand, including entities outside Thailand offering goods or services to or monitoring people there.
scope_summary: Applies to collection, use and disclosure of personal data in Thailand, with extraterritorial reach for offering goods or services to, or monitoring behavior of, individuals in Thailand.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a lawful basis, explicit consent for sensitive personal data, privacy notices and support for data subject rights including access, portability, erasure and objection. Controllers must maintain records of processing activities, implement security measures and notify the Office of the PDPC of personal data breaches within 72 hours where feasible. A data protection officer and a local representative are required in specified cases, and cross-border transfers need adequate protection or an approved mechanism.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|consent records|records of processing|DPO appointment|breach notifications|transfer safeguards|security policies
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; program review commonly annual
penalties_summary: Administrative fines up to 5 million Thai baht, plus civil liability including punitive damages and criminal penalties for specified sensitive-data violations.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured by statutory chapters on lawful bases, rights, controller and processor duties, transfers and enforcement.

name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information
source_note: Japan's personal information protection law, adequacy-recognized by the European Commission
who_must_comply: Personal information handling business operators in Japan and foreign businesses that handle personal information of people in Japan in connection with supplying goods or services.
scope_summary: Applies to handling of personal information, pseudonymously processed information and anonymously processed information by business operators, with extraterritorial application.
key_obligations_summary: Requires specification and notification of utilization purposes, limits on use and third-party provision, security control measures and records for third-party transfers. Operators must respond to disclosure, correction and cessation requests, and must report leaks that risk individual rights to the Personal Information Protection Commission and notify affected individuals. Cross-border transfers require consent with prescribed information, an adequacy finding or equivalent safeguards with ongoing verification.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy policy|purpose notifications|transfer records|security control measures documentation|breach reports|consent records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; the APPI is reviewed by the PPC roughly every three years
penalties_summary: Fines up to 100 million Japanese yen for corporations for specified violations such as failing to comply with a PPC order, plus penalties for individuals.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are organized by statutory duties covering purpose, acquisition, security, third-party provision, cross-border transfer and individual rights.

name: Personal Information Protection Act (Korea)
source_note: South Korea's comprehensive privacy law with strict consent and cross-border transfer rules
who_must_comply: Any personal information controller in Korea, public or private, and overseas entities processing Korean residents' personal data in scope of the Act.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal information of Korean data subjects, including pseudonymized data rules and specific provisions for overseas transfers.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a specific legal basis, typically granular consent, privacy notices, and support for rights including access, correction, deletion and suspension of processing. Controllers must appoint a privacy officer, implement prescribed technical and administrative safeguards, and report data breaches to the PIPC and affected individuals within statutory deadlines. Overseas transfers require consent or another listed basis, and the PIPC can order transfer suspension.
typical_evidence_artifacts: consent records|privacy notice|privacy officer designation|safeguard measures documentation|breach reports|overseas transfer documentation|impact assessments
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; privacy impact assessments and audits per regulation
penalties_summary: Administrative fines up to 3 percent of total related revenue for serious violations, plus penalty surcharges and criminal penalties for specified breaches.
subordinate_controls_notes: Statutory duties plus enforcement decree safeguards; the ISMS-P certification scheme is often used as supporting evidence.

name: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (India)
source_note: India's consent-based personal data law; implementation via DPDP Rules is phased
who_must_comply: Data fiduciaries processing digital personal data within India, and those outside India processing such data in connection with offering goods or services to people in India.
scope_summary: Applies to digital personal data, including data digitized after collection, with exemptions for certain government processing and publicly available data.
key_obligations_summary: Requires clear notice and consent or a legitimate use basis, appointment of a consent manager where used, and honoring rights to access, correction, erasure and grievance redressal. Data fiduciaries must implement reasonable security safeguards, notify the Data Protection Board and affected data principals of breaches, and observe additional duties for children's data. Significant data fiduciaries face extra obligations including a data protection officer in India, independent audits and impact assessments, with timelines set by the DPDP Rules.
typical_evidence_artifacts: consent notices and records|privacy notice|breach notifications|security safeguards documentation|DPIA and audit reports for significant data fiduciaries|grievance records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; annual independent audit for significant data fiduciaries
penalties_summary: Financial penalties up to 2.5 billion Indian rupees per specified breach, including up to 2.5 billion rupees for failure to take reasonable security safeguards.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are set by statute and the DPDP Rules, with heightened duties for significant data fiduciaries rather than a control catalog.

name: Protection of Personal Information Act
source_note: South Africa's data protection law enforced by the Information Regulator
who_must_comply: Public and private bodies that process personal information of data subjects in South Africa, including juristic persons.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal information entered in a record by or for a responsible party domiciled in South Africa, or using means in South Africa.
key_obligations_summary: Requires compliance with eight conditions for lawful processing covering accountability, processing limitation, purpose specification, further processing limitation, information quality, openness, security safeguards and data subject participation. Responsible parties must register an Information Officer with the Information Regulator, maintain security measures and notify the Regulator and data subjects of security compromises. Special personal information and children's data require additional authorization, and cross-border transfers require a listed basis.
typical_evidence_artifacts: PAIA and privacy manual|Information Officer registration|processing records|security safeguards documentation|breach notifications|operator agreements
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; program review commonly annual
penalties_summary: Administrative fines up to 10 million South African rand and criminal penalties including imprisonment of up to ten years for the most serious offences.
subordinate_controls_notes: Eight conditions for lawful processing, supported by regulations and Information Regulator guidance.

name: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
source_note: Nigerian data protection statute signed June 2023; implemented through the 2025 General Application and Implementation Directive
who_must_comply: Data controllers and processors processing personal data of data subjects in Nigeria, including foreign entities processing such data.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal data where the controller or processor is in Nigeria, processes Nigerian residents' data, or targets people in Nigeria.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a lawful basis, transparency, and support for data subject rights including access, rectification, erasure and objection. Controllers and processors of major importance must register with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, appoint a data protection officer and conduct compliance audits. Security breaches must be reported to the Commission within 72 hours, and cross-border transfers require an adequacy determination or another statutory basis.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy policy|registration with the NDPC|DPO appointment|compliance audit report|breach notifications|processing records|transfer documentation
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual compliance audit filing for controllers of major importance
penalties_summary: Penalties up to the greater of 10 million Nigerian naira and 2 percent of annual gross revenue for data controllers of major importance, with lower tiers for others.
subordinate_controls_notes: Obligations are structured by statutory principles plus the General Application and Implementation Directive.

name: Saudi Personal Data Protection Law
issuing_body: Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA)
source_note: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia personal data law with implementing regulations and transfer rules issued by SDAIA
who_must_comply: Any entity processing personal data of individuals residing in Saudi Arabia, including entities outside the Kingdom processing such data.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal data in Saudi Arabia by public and private entities, with extraterritorial reach for data of residents.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a lawful basis, privacy notices, records of processing and registration on the SDAIA national platform where required, plus support for rights of access, correction and destruction. Controllers must conduct impact assessments for higher-risk processing, appoint a personal data protection officer in specified cases, and notify SDAIA of breaches within 72 hours. Cross-border transfers require compliance with the transfer regulations, including risk assessments and, in some cases, appropriate safeguards.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|records of processing|registration records|impact assessments|breach notifications|transfer risk assessments|processor agreements
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; registration and assessments refreshed per SDAIA rules
penalties_summary: Fines up to 5 million Saudi riyals, doubled for repeat violations, with criminal penalties including imprisonment for unlawful disclosure of sensitive data.
subordinate_controls_notes: Statutory obligations detailed by the Implementing Regulation and the Regulation on Personal Data Transfer outside the Kingdom.

name: UAE Personal Data Protection Law
also_known_as: UAE PDPL; Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021
source_note: UAE federal personal data protection regime; DIFC and ADGM free zones maintain separate data protection laws
who_must_comply: Entities processing personal data of data subjects inside the UAE and, in specified cases, controllers or processors outside the UAE processing UAE data subjects' data.
scope_summary: Applies onshore in the UAE outside free zones with their own regimes; the DIFC Data Protection Law and ADGM Data Protection Regulations apply separately within those financial free zones.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a lawful basis or consent meeting statutory conditions, privacy notices, records of processing and support for rights including access, correction, erasure, portability and objection. Controllers must implement appropriate security measures, notify the UAE Data Office and affected individuals of breaches without undue delay, and appoint a data protection officer in specified higher-risk cases. Cross-border transfers require an adequate destination or specified safeguards such as contractual clauses.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|records of processing|DPO appointment where required|breach notifications|transfer safeguards|processor agreements
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; program review commonly annual
penalties_summary: Administrative penalties are set by Cabinet decision; specific fine amounts for the federal PDPL are unknown pending publication, while DIFC and ADGM regimes publish their own fine schedules.
subordinate_controls_notes: Federal statutory duties, with separate control regimes in the DIFC and ADGM free zones.

name: Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection
issuing_body: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (Switzerland)
source_note: Revised Swiss data protection act in force since September 2023, closely aligned with the GDPR
who_must_comply: Organizations processing personal data of people in Switzerland, including foreign companies whose processing has effects in Switzerland.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal data of natural persons by private persons and federal bodies, with extraterritorial effect for processing that affects Switzerland.
key_obligations_summary: Requires transparency, proportionality and purpose limitation, a register of processing activities for many organizations, data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing and privacy by design and default. Data security breaches that pose a high risk must be reported to the FDPIC as soon as possible. Transfers abroad require adequacy, contractual safeguards such as SCCs with Swiss adaptations, or another legal basis, and some foreign controllers must appoint a Swiss representative.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notice|register of processing activities|DPIA|processor contracts|SCCs with Swiss addendum|breach records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; assessments reviewed on material change
penalties_summary: Criminal fines of up to 250,000 Swiss francs imposed on responsible individuals for specified breaches, rather than corporate administrative fines.
subordinate_controls_notes: Structured by statutory duties covering principles, information, rights, security, DPIAs and cross-border transfers.

name: Turkish Personal Data Protection Law
source_note: Turkey's personal data protection law with registration (VERBIS) and transfer requirements
who_must_comply: Data controllers processing personal data of individuals in Turkey, including foreign controllers targeting Turkey.
scope_summary: Applies to processing of personal data of natural persons in Turkey by controllers and processors, wholly or partly by automated means.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a lawful basis, explicit consent for special categories unless an exception applies, privacy notices, and registration in the VERBIS data controllers registry unless exempt. Controllers must respond to data subject applications within 30 days, take technical and organizational measures, and notify the Authority within 72 hours of learning of a data breach. Cross-border transfers rely on adequacy, standard contracts filed with the Authority, binding corporate rules or explicit consent under the amended transfer regime.
typical_evidence_artifacts: privacy notices|VERBIS registration|personal data inventory|data retention and destruction policy|breach notifications|standard contracts for transfers
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous; VERBIS entries and inventories updated on change
penalties_summary: Administrative fines set annually by statute and adjusted for inflation, ranging by violation type; amounts for the current year are published by the Authority.
subordinate_controls_notes: Statutory duties plus Authority decisions and the technical and organizational measures guidance.

name: NERC CIP Standards
also_known_as: NERC Critical Infrastructure Protection; CIP-002 through CIP-015
source_note: Mandatory, enforceable cyber and physical security standards for the bulk electric system
who_must_comply: Owners and operators of the North American bulk electric system, and vendors supplying systems inside their compliance scope.
scope_summary: Applies to BES Cyber Systems and associated assets categorized as high, medium or low impact.
key_obligations_summary: Requires categorization of BES cyber systems and implementation of standards covering security management controls, personnel and training, electronic security perimeters, physical security, system security management, incident reporting, recovery, configuration change management, information protection and supply chain risk. Compliance is enforced by NERC and regional entities through audits and self-reports. Registered entities must retain evidence for defined periods.
typical_evidence_artifacts: asset categorization|CIP policies|access authorization records|configuration baselines|patch evaluations|incident reports|audit evidence
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: continuous with periodic regional audits, commonly on a 3-year cycle
penalties_summary: Civil penalties up to the statutory maximum per violation per day under FERC-approved enforcement, which is over one million U.S. dollars per day per violation.
subordinate_controls_notes: Standards CIP-002 through CIP-015 cover categorization, personnel, perimeters, physical security, system management, incident response, recovery, change management, information protection, supply chain and internal network monitoring.

name: TSA Cybersecurity Security Directives
also_known_as: TSA pipeline security directives; TSA rail security directives
source_note: Mandatory cybersecurity directives for designated pipeline, rail, and aviation owners and operators
who_must_comply: Owners and operators of TSA-designated critical pipeline, freight and passenger rail, and higher-risk aviation systems in the United States.
scope_summary: Covers designated critical cyber systems, including information technology and operational technology systems supporting the regulated operations.
key_obligations_summary: Requires designation of a cybersecurity coordinator, reporting of cybersecurity incidents to CISA generally within 24 hours, a cybersecurity assessment plan with annual testing of controls, and a TSA-approved cybersecurity implementation plan including network segmentation, access control, continuous monitoring and patching. Owners and operators must submit plans for approval and report on assessment results. Directives are periodically renewed and updated, and TSA has proposed a permanent rule.
typical_evidence_artifacts: cybersecurity implementation plan|cybersecurity assessment plan and annual results|incident reports to CISA|cybersecurity coordinator designation|network segmentation architecture|patch management records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual assessment testing, with directive renewals typically annual
penalties_summary: TSA civil penalties per violation under its aviation and surface transportation authorities, with amounts adjusted for inflation and enforcement including operational directives.
subordinate_controls_notes: Requirements are organized around implementation and assessment plans with control areas such as segmentation, access control, monitoring and patching.

name: Food Safety Modernization Act
source_note: Preventive controls and traceability requirements for food facilities
who_must_comply: Domestic and foreign facilities that manufacture, process, pack or hold food for U.S. consumption, plus importers, farms and, for traceability, entities handling listed foods.
scope_summary: Covers human and animal food operations subject to FDA jurisdiction, with exemptions and modified requirements for qualified small businesses.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a written food safety plan with hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls, monitoring, corrective actions, verification and records, implemented under Part 117. Importers must operate a Foreign Supplier Verification Program, and produce safety, sanitary transportation and intentional adulteration rules apply to relevant operations. The Food Traceability Rule requires additional records and traceability lot codes for listed foods, with the compliance date extended to July 2028.
typical_evidence_artifacts: food safety plan|hazard analysis|monitoring and verification records|supplier approval and FSVP records|training records (PCQI)|traceability records and lot codes|recall plan
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: food safety plan reanalysis at least every 3 years and on significant change
penalties_summary: No fixed fine schedule; FDA actions include warning letters, mandatory recall, administrative detention, import refusal, suspension of registration, injunction and criminal prosecution.
subordinate_controls_notes: Requirements are organized by rule, including preventive controls, FSVP, produce safety, sanitary transportation, intentional adulteration and traceability.

name: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point
source_note: Preventive food safety management system required for certain FDA- and USDA-regulated products
who_must_comply: Seafood and juice processors under FDA rules and meat, poultry and egg product establishments under USDA rules, plus organizations adopting HACCP voluntarily or by customer requirement.
scope_summary: Covers food production processes and the identification and control of biological, chemical and physical hazards at critical control points.
key_obligations_summary: Requires a hazard analysis, identification of critical control points with critical limits, monitoring procedures, corrective actions, verification activities and recordkeeping. Mandatory application arises under FDA seafood and juice HACCP regulations and USDA FSIS rules, while other sectors adopt it voluntarily or under buyer schemes such as GFSI-recognized standards. Plans must be validated and reassessed when processes change.
typical_evidence_artifacts: HACCP plan|hazard analysis|critical control point monitoring records|corrective action records|verification and validation records|sanitation SOPs|training records
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: reassessment at least annually or when the process changes
penalties_summary: No fixed fine schedule; regulators can suspend inspection, detain or refuse product, issue warning letters and pursue injunction or prosecution.
subordinate_controls_notes: Seven principles: hazard analysis, critical control point determination, critical limits, monitoring, corrective actions, verification and recordkeeping.

name: TL 9000
also_known_as: TL 9000 Quality Management System; QuEST Forum
source_note: Telecommunications-sector quality management system built on ISO 9001 with industry measurements
who_must_comply: Telecommunications equipment, software and service suppliers whose customers require sector-specific quality certification.
scope_summary: Covers the quality management system for telecom products and services in the declared scope, including hardware, software and services categories.
key_obligations_summary: Builds on ISO 9001 with telecom-specific adders and requires submission of standardized performance measurements to the industry measurement repository. Certification is issued by accredited certification bodies following audit. Measurement reporting is a distinguishing ongoing obligation compared with plain ISO 9001.
typical_evidence_artifacts: quality manual|ISO 9001 and TL 9000 adder documentation|measurement submissions to the repository|corrective action records|internal audit reports|certificate
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: every 3 years with annual surveillance audits and ongoing monthly or quarterly measurement submissions
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; loss of certification can remove suppliers from telecom carriers' approved vendor lists.
subordinate_controls_notes: ISO 9001 requirements plus TL 9000 hardware, software and services adders and the measurements handbook.

name: SASB Standards
source_note: Industry-specific sustainability disclosure standards now maintained under the IFRS Foundation
who_must_comply: Companies making sustainability disclosures to investors, particularly those reporting under IFRS S1 and S2 or responding to investor requests.
scope_summary: Covers industry-specific sustainability topics and metrics across 77 industries, focused on financially material information for investors.
key_obligations_summary: Provides disclosure topics and accounting metrics by industry that companies use to report financially material sustainability information. The standards are voluntary in themselves but are referenced by IFRS S1 for identifying industry-specific risks, opportunities and metrics. They are maintained by the ISSB under the IFRS Foundation.
typical_evidence_artifacts: materiality assessment|industry metric disclosures|data collection methodology|internal controls over sustainability data|assurance report where obtained
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty in themselves; misstatements can create securities liability where disclosures are made to investors.
subordinate_controls_notes: Organized by industry with disclosure topics, accounting metrics and activity metrics.

name: GRI Standards
source_note: Widely used voluntary sustainability reporting standards
who_must_comply: Organizations of any size reporting sustainability impacts to a broad range of stakeholders, often alongside investor-focused standards.
scope_summary: Covers an organization's most significant impacts on the economy, environment and people, including human rights, using an impact materiality lens.
key_obligations_summary: Requires reporting in accordance with universal standards covering context, material topics and management approach, supplemented by sector and topic standards. Organizations determine material topics through an impact materiality process and disclose management approach and metrics. Use is voluntary and self-declared, with third-party assurance optional.
typical_evidence_artifacts: materiality assessment|GRI content index|topic disclosures|stakeholder engagement records|data methodology documentation|assurance report where obtained
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No statutory penalty; inaccurate claims can create consumer protection or securities exposure depending on use.
subordinate_controls_notes: Universal Standards GRI 1, 2 and 3, plus sector standards and topic standards.

name: IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards
also_known_as: IFRS S1; IFRS S2; ISSB standards
issuing_body: International Sustainability Standards Board, IFRS Foundation
source_note: Global baseline sustainability and climate disclosure standards adopted by many jurisdictions
who_must_comply: Companies in jurisdictions that have adopted or endorsed ISSB standards, and companies voluntarily providing investor-focused sustainability disclosures.
scope_summary: Covers sustainability-related risks and opportunities that could reasonably be expected to affect an entity's cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital, with IFRS S2 focused on climate.
key_obligations_summary: Requires disclosure of governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets for material sustainability-related risks and opportunities, aligned with the TCFD structure. IFRS S2 adds climate-specific requirements including Scope 1, 2 and, subject to relief, Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions measured using the GHG Protocol, plus climate resilience analysis. Legal force depends on each jurisdiction's adoption decisions and timelines.
typical_evidence_artifacts: governance and oversight documentation|climate risk and scenario analysis|GHG inventory (Scope 1, 2, 3)|metrics and targets disclosures|data controls documentation|assurance report where required
renewal_or_reassessment_cadence: annual
penalties_summary: No penalty from the ISSB; consequences arise from national securities and reporting regimes that adopt the standards.
subordinate_controls_notes: Core content pillars of governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets, with industry-based guidance derived from SASB.
